java-code-total-seconds.title: Total seconds
java-code-total-seconds.description:
Your first real Java method. In class `Solution`, write

```java
static int totalSeconds(int hours, int minutes, int seconds)
```

that returns the length of a time span in seconds. One hour is 3600 seconds and one minute is 60.

**Examples** `totalSeconds(0, 1, 30)` → `90`; `totalSeconds(2, 0, 5)` → `7205`.

All arguments are between 0 and 1000, so the result fits in an `int`.

*Java problems are compiled and run on a judge server: you need to be logged in to submit.*

guide.prereqs: Lessons *From source code to a running program* and *Anatomy of a class, main, and your first statements*.
guide.intuition: Convert each part to seconds and add them up.
hints: An hour is 60 minutes of 60 seconds each.
`*` is done before `+`, so no parentheses are needed.
`return hours * 3600 + minutes * 60 + seconds;`
guide.brute_force: You could loop, adding 3600 once per hour and 60 once per minute. It works and does needless work; multiplication says it directly.
guide.complexity: Time O(1), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Multiplying hours by 60 instead of 3600.
- Forgetting the `return`.
- For much larger inputs an `int` would overflow; `long` would be needed.

java-code-average.title: Average of three
java-code-average.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static double average(int a, int b, int c)
```

returning the exact arithmetic mean of three whole numbers.

**Examples** `average(1, 2, 4)` → `2.3333333333333335`; `average(3, 3, 3)` → `3.0`.

The trap: `(a + b + c) / 3` divides two `int` values, so Java throws the fraction away. Make sure the
division happens in `double`. The arguments may be as large as `Integer.MAX_VALUE`, so their sum may not fit
in an `int`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Primitive types and how numbers are stored*: integer division, overflow, widening.
guide.intuition: Two separate dangers: the sum can overflow `int`, and the division can lose its fraction. Widen to `long` before adding and divide by a `double`.
hints: `3.0` is a `double` literal; dividing by it gives a `double` result.
Cast one operand to `long` before the additions so that they are done in 64 bits.
guide.brute_force: Writing `(a + b + c) / 3` is the natural first attempt. It returns `2.0` for (1, 2, 4).
guide.complexity: Time O(1), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Integer division.
- `(double) (a + b + c) / 3`: the cast is applied after the `int` sum has already overflowed.
- Casting the result instead of an operand.

java-code-initials.title: Initials
java-code-initials.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static String initials(String fullName)
```

Return the first letter of each word in upper case, each followed by a dot.

- Words are separated by one or more spaces; there may be spaces at the start or end.
- An empty or all-space name gives the empty string `""`.

**Examples** `initials("ada lovelace")` → `"A.L."`; `initials("  Grace   Brewster Hopper ")` → `"G.B.H."`;
`initials("")` → `""`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Packages, imports and the String toolbox*: `trim`, `split`, `charAt`, `StringBuilder`.
guide.intuition: Cut the name into words, take each word's first character, upper-case it, and build the answer piece by piece.
hints: `trim()` removes the spaces at both ends.
`split(" +")` splits on runs of one or more spaces (the argument is a regular expression).
`"".split(" +")` returns one empty string, so skip empty words.
guide.brute_force: Walk the characters with a flag 'previous character was a space'; whenever a non-space follows a space (or the start), it is an initial. Equally fast, and it avoids regular expressions.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) in the length of the name, space O(n).
guide.pitfalls:
- `split(" ")` produces empty strings for double spaces, and `charAt(0)` on an empty string throws `StringIndexOutOfBoundsException`.
- Forgetting to upper-case.
- Building with `+=` in a loop works here but is the habit `StringBuilder` replaces.

java-code-leap-year.title: Leap year
java-code-leap-year.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static boolean isLeapYear(int year)
```

A year is a leap year if it is divisible by 4, **except** years divisible by 100, which are leap years only
if they are also divisible by 400.

**Examples** `isLeapYear(2024)` → `true`; `isLeapYear(1900)` → `false`; `isLeapYear(2000)` → `true`;
`isLeapYear(2023)` → `false`. `year` is at least 1.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Anatomy of a class, main, and your first statements*: `if`, comparison and the logical operators `&&`, `||`.
guide.intuition: Translate the sentence into a boolean expression: divisible by 4 AND (not divisible by 100 OR divisible by 400).
hints: `year % 4 == 0` tests divisibility by 4.
The exception has its own exception, so parentheses are needed.
A boolean expression can be returned directly; no `if` is required.
guide.brute_force: Three nested `if` statements, from the most specific rule (400) to the least (4), give the same answer and are easier to read for some people.
guide.complexity: Time O(1), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Stopping at 'divisible by 4'.
- Forgetting the 400 rule.
- Missing parentheses: `&&` binds tighter than `||`.

java-code-fizzbuzz.title: FizzBuzz
java-code-fizzbuzz.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static String fizzBuzz(int n)
```

For the numbers 1 to `n`, produce one token each, separated by single spaces (no space at the end):

- `"FizzBuzz"` if the number is divisible by both 3 and 5;
- `"Fizz"` if divisible by 3;
- `"Buzz"` if divisible by 5;
- otherwise the number itself.

For `n <= 0` return `""`.

**Example** `fizzBuzz(5)` → `"1 2 Fizz 4 Buzz"`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Loops, operators and casting*: the counting `for` loop and `%`.
guide.intuition: Loop from 1 to n, decide the token for each number, and join the tokens with spaces. The only subtlety is testing the most specific condition first.
hints: Test divisibility by 15 before 3 and 5.
Append a space before every token except the first.
Use a `StringBuilder` and return `sb.toString()`.
guide.brute_force: Collect the tokens in a `List<String>` and call `String.join(" ", tokens)`: slightly more memory, and no separator bookkeeping.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the result.
guide.pitfalls:
- Testing 3 before 15, so 15 prints `Fizz`.
- `i < n` instead of `i <= n`.
- A trailing space.

java-code-count-vowels.title: Count vowels
java-code-count-vowels.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static int countVowels(String text)
```

returning how many characters of `text` are vowels: `a`, `e`, `i`, `o`, `u`, in either upper or lower case.

**Examples** `countVowels("Education")` → `5`; `countVowels("rhythm")` → `0`; `countVowels("")` → `0`.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Loops, operators and casting* and *Packages, imports and the String toolbox*.
guide.intuition: Visit every character once and count those that belong to a small set.
hints: Loop with an index from 0 to `text.length() - 1` and read `text.charAt(i)`.
Convert each character to lower case first, so one comparison handles both cases.
`"aeiou".indexOf(c) >= 0` is a compact membership test.
guide.brute_force: Count each vowel separately with five passes over the text. Correct, and five times the work.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1) (O(n) if you copy to a char array).
guide.pitfalls:
- Counting only lower-case vowels.
- Starting the index at 1.
- Comparing a `char` with a `String` such as `"a"`: use single quotes for characters.

java-code-index-of-max.title: Index of the largest element
java-code-index-of-max.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static int indexOfMax(int[] values)
```

Return the index of the largest element. If the largest value occurs several times, return the **first**
such index. For an empty array return `-1`.

**Examples** `indexOfMax(new int[] {3, 9, 2, 9})` → `1`; `indexOfMax(new int[] {})` → `-1`;
`indexOfMax(new int[] {-5, -2, -8})` → `1`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *References, arrays, the stack and the heap*: arrays, indices and `length`.
guide.intuition: Keep the index of the best element seen so far, starting with the first element, and replace it only when a strictly larger one appears.
hints: Handle the empty array before the loop.
Start with `best = 0` and loop from index 1.
Use `>` and not `>=`, so that ties keep the earlier index.
guide.brute_force: Find the maximum value in one pass and its first position in a second pass. Two passes, same result.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Initialising the running maximum to 0, which fails for arrays of negative numbers.
- `>=`, which returns the last maximum.
- Reading `values[0]` of an empty array.

java-code-reverse-array.title: Reversed copy of an array
java-code-reverse-array.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static int[] reversed(int[] values)
```

Return a **new** array holding the elements of `values` in reverse order. The array passed in must be left
unchanged.

**Examples** `reversed(new int[] {1, 2, 3})` → `{3, 2, 1}`; `reversed(new int[] {})` → `{}`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *References, arrays, the stack and the heap*: arrays are objects; a method receives a copy of the reference.
guide.intuition: Because the caller's array is the same object the method sees, reversing 'in place' would change the caller's data. Allocate a second array and fill it from the far end.
hints: `new int[n]` creates the result.
Element `i` of the result is element `n - 1 - i` of the input.
Return the new array, never `values`.
guide.brute_force: Copy with `values.clone()` and then swap pairs inside the copy from both ends: also fine, and it uses the swap idiom.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n) for the new array.
guide.pitfalls:
- Reversing the caller's array.
- `values[n - i]`, an off-by-one that throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException` at `i = 0`.
- Returning the input for the empty case is tempting; a new empty array keeps the contract simple.

java-code-is-palindrome.title: Palindrome, ignoring punctuation
java-code-is-palindrome.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static boolean isPalindrome(String text)
```

Return `true` if `text` reads the same forwards and backwards when you consider **only letters and digits**
and ignore case. A text with no letters or digits counts as a palindrome.

**Examples** `isPalindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")` → `true`; `isPalindrome("race a car")` → `false`;
`isPalindrome("")` → `true`.

Useful library methods: `Character.isLetterOrDigit(c)` and `Character.toLowerCase(c)`.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Methods, parameters, return values and pass-by-value* and *Loops, operators and casting*.
guide.intuition: Two fingers, one at each end, walking toward each other. Skip anything that is not a letter or digit; compare what remains.
hints: Use two indices `i` and `j`.
If the character at `i` should be ignored, move `i`; likewise for `j`.
When both are significant, compare in lower case; on a mismatch return `false` at once.
guide.brute_force: Build a cleaned string (letters and digits only, lower-cased) with a `StringBuilder`, then compare it with its reverse. Simple and correct, with O(n) extra memory.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Comparing the raw string with its reverse, which respects case and punctuation.
- Ignoring digits.
- Letting the indices cross and read out of bounds.

java-code-bank-account.title: A class with state: Account
java-code-bank-account.description:
Write your first class with **encapsulated state**. Inside `Solution`, complete the nested class `Account`:

```java
static class Account {
    Account(String owner)           // balance starts at 0
    String owner()
    long balance()                  // in pence
    void deposit(long pence)        // throws IllegalArgumentException if pence <= 0
    boolean withdraw(long pence)    // if pence <= 0 or pence > balance: change nothing, return false; else subtract, return true
}
```

Keep the fields `private`. Each `Account` object must have its own balance.

**Example**

```java
Solution.Account a = new Solution.Account("Noor");
a.deposit(500);
a.withdraw(200);     // true
a.withdraw(900);     // false
a.balance();         // 300
```

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Classes and objects: blueprint and building* and *Encapsulation: private fields, getters and setters*.
guide.intuition: The class guards one rule (an invariant): the balance never goes below zero. Because the field is private, only `deposit` and `withdraw` can change it, so the rule is checked in exactly two places.
hints: Two fields: `private final String owner` and `private long balance`.
`this.owner = owner;` in the constructor distinguishes the field from the parameter.
In `withdraw`, test the failing conditions first and return `false` before changing anything.
guide.brute_force: Public fields would 'work' and would let any code set a negative balance. The point of the exercise is that the class, not its callers, enforces the rule.
guide.complexity: Every method is O(1); each object uses O(1) space.
guide.pitfalls:
- Declaring `balance` as `static`, so that all accounts share one balance.
- Subtracting first and checking afterwards, which leaves the account overdrawn.
- Forgetting to validate `deposit`.

java-code-ticket-counter.title: static versus instance: Ticket
java-code-ticket-counter.description:
Inside `Solution`, complete the nested class `Ticket` so that every new ticket receives the next number.

```java
static class Ticket {
    Ticket()                 // takes the next number
    int number()             // this ticket's number
    static int issued()      // how many tickets have been created so far
    static void reset()      // start again: issued() becomes 0 and the next ticket gets number 1
}
```

The first ticket after a reset has number 1, the second 2, and so on. `issued()` must work even when no
ticket exists. A ticket keeps its number for ever, even after later tickets are created or `reset` is called.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *static, final, constants and the Math class*: one copy per class versus one copy per object.
guide.intuition: The running count belongs to the class as a whole, so it is `static`. Each ticket's own number belongs to that ticket, so it is an instance field, copied from the counter at construction.
hints: `private static int issued` is shared by all tickets.
In the constructor: increment the shared counter, then store its value in `private final int number`.
`number()` returns the instance field, not the counter.
guide.brute_force: Returning the static counter from `number()` is the usual first mistake: every ticket would then report the latest number.
guide.complexity: All operations O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Making the per-ticket number static.
- Making the counter an instance field: every ticket would be number 1.
- Calling an instance method from a static one without an object.

java-code-shapes.title: An interface and two implementations
java-code-shapes.description:
Inside `Solution` you are given the interface

```java
interface Shape {
    double area();
    String name();
}
```

Write two nested classes that implement it, and one method that works with **any** shape:

```java
static class Circle implements Shape     // Circle(double radius);         area = Math.PI * r * r;  name() returns "circle"
static class Rect implements Shape       // Rect(double width, double height);  area = w * h;       name() returns "rect"
static double totalArea(java.util.List<Shape> shapes)                 // sum of the areas; 0 for an empty list
static String largest(java.util.List<Shape> shapes)                   // name() of the shape with the largest area; "" for an empty list
```

`totalArea` and `largest` must not test which class a shape is; they call `area()` and `name()` and let
dynamic dispatch do the rest. If two shapes tie for largest, return the name of the one that comes first.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Interfaces, default methods, sealed types and pattern matching* and *Polymorphism, overriding and overloading*.
guide.intuition: The interface is the contract; `totalArea` and `largest` are written against the contract alone. The tests pass in a shape class your code has never seen, which only works if you call `area()` and do not ask what kind of shape it is.
hints: Implementing methods must be `public`.
Loop over `List<Shape>` and call `s.area()`; the object's own class decides which code runs.
For `largest`, keep the best shape so far and replace it only on a strictly larger area.
guide.brute_force: A chain of `instanceof` tests handles the two known shapes and silently ignores every other implementation. It is exactly the design the open/closed principle warns about.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) for both methods, space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Forgetting `public` on the implementing methods (a compile error).
- Type-testing inside `totalArea`.
- Circumference `2πr` instead of area `πr²`.
- `>=` in `largest`, which returns the last of several equal shapes.

java-code-employee-pay.title: Abstract class and overriding: payroll
java-code-employee-pay.description:
Inside `Solution`, build a small hierarchy.

```java
static abstract class Employee {
    Employee(String name)
    String name()
    abstract int weeklyPay();                    // in pounds
    String payslip()                             // returns name() + ": " + weeklyPay()   (written ONCE, here)
}

static class Salaried extends Employee          // Salaried(String name, int annualSalary);  weeklyPay = annualSalary / 52 (integer division)
static class Hourly extends Employee            // Hourly(String name, int ratePerHour, int hours)
                                                //   first 40 hours at the rate, hours beyond 40 at DOUBLE the rate
static class Manager extends Salaried           // Manager(String name, int annualSalary, int weeklyBonus)
                                                //   weeklyPay = the Salaried weekly pay + weeklyBonus  (reuse it with super)

static int payroll(java.util.List<Employee> staff)     // sum of weeklyPay()
```

**Example** `new Hourly("Bo", 10, 45).weeklyPay()` → `500` (40 × 10 + 5 × 20);
`new Manager("Cy", 52000, 150).payslip()` → `"Cy: 1150"`.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Inheritance: sharing code through a family tree*, *Abstract classes and the Object class* and *Constructors, this and super*.
guide.intuition: `Employee` fixes what every employee has (a name, a payslip format) and leaves one question open: how is the pay computed? Each subclass answers that single question. `payslip()` calls `weeklyPay()` and dynamic dispatch picks the right answer.
hints: Each subclass constructor must call `super(...)` first, because `Employee` has no no-argument constructor.
`Hourly`: split the hours into the first 40 and the rest.
`Manager` should not recompute the salary: `super.weeklyPay() + weeklyBonus`.
guide.brute_force: A single `Employee` class with a `type` field and a `switch` in `weeklyPay` works for three kinds and has to be edited for every new kind: the tagged-class design the hierarchy replaces.
guide.complexity: Each `weeklyPay` is O(1); `payroll` is O(n).
guide.pitfalls:
- Forgetting `super(name)`: 'constructor Employee cannot be applied to given types'.
- Paying overtime at the normal rate.
- Adding the weekly bonus to the annual salary before dividing.
- Duplicating `payslip` in every subclass.

java-code-safe-divide.title: Catching exceptions: parse and divide
java-code-safe-divide.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static String divide(String a, String b)
```

`a` and `b` are text typed by a user. Parse both with `Integer.parseInt` and return the result of the
integer division `a / b` as text. Handle the two things that can go wrong:

- if either text is not a valid whole number, return `"not a number"`;
- if the divisor is zero, return `"division by zero"`.

Use `try` and `catch`; do not test for zero or validate the digits yourself.

**Examples** `divide("17", "5")` → `"3"`; `divide("17", "five")` → `"not a number"`;
`divide("17", "0")` → `"division by zero"`; `divide("-7", "2")` → `"-3"`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Exceptions: try, catch, finally, checked and unchecked*.
guide.intuition: Write the happy path as if nothing could go wrong, inside `try`. Then add one `catch` for each kind of failure, each returning its own message.
hints: `Integer.parseInt` throws `NumberFormatException` for bad text.
Integer division by zero throws `ArithmeticException`.
Two separate catch blocks; each exception type selects its block.
guide.brute_force: Checking the text with a regular expression and testing `b == 0` by hand also works. Here the aim is to practise the mechanism the library already gives you.
guide.complexity: Time O(length of the inputs), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- One broad `catch (Exception e)`, which cannot tell the two failures apart.
- Casting to `double`: floating-point division by zero does not throw, it gives `Infinity`.
- Trimming the input changes which texts are accepted.

java-code-wallet-exception.title: A custom checked exception

guide.prereqs: Lessons *try-with-resources, multi-catch and custom exceptions*, *Choosing exceptions* and *Documenting, detailing and recovering from failures*.
guide.intuition: A declined payment is something a caller can recover from, so it is a checked exception carrying the data needed for recovery (the shortfall). A negative price is a bug in the caller, so it is an unchecked `IllegalArgumentException`. Check everything before changing the balance, so a failed call changes nothing.
hints: `extends Exception` makes it checked; pass the message to `super(...)`.
`pay` must declare `throws InsufficientFundsException`.
Validate first, mutate last: that gives failure atomicity.
guide.brute_force: Returning `false` or `-1` from `pay` avoids exceptions but loses the shortfall and lets callers ignore the failure. The exception carries the detail and cannot be skipped by accident.
guide.complexity: All operations O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Extending `RuntimeException`: the exception becomes unchecked and callers are no longer forced to handle it.
- Subtracting before checking, leaving a negative balance after a failed payment.
- No `throws` clause on `pay`: the compiler rejects throwing a checked exception without it.

java-code-dedupe-list.title: Remove duplicates, keep the order
java-code-dedupe-list.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static List<Integer> dedupe(List<Integer> values)
```

Return a **new** list containing each distinct value once, in the order of its **first** appearance. Do not
modify the list you were given (it may be unmodifiable).

**Examples** `dedupe(List.of(3, 1, 3, 2, 1))` → `[3, 1, 2]`; `dedupe(List.of())` → `[]`.

The values may be large (such as 1000), so compare them by value, never with `==` on `Integer` objects.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *ArrayList and reading the API documentation* and *Collections: List, Set, Map and Queue*.
guide.intuition: A set rejects duplicates; a `LinkedHashSet` also remembers insertion order. Pour the list into one and pour it back out.
hints: Which `Set` implementation keeps insertion order?
`new LinkedHashSet<>(values)` copies and removes duplicates in one step.
Wrap the set in `new ArrayList<>(...)` to return a list.
guide.brute_force: For each value, scan the output list built so far and add the value only if it is absent: O(n²), and correct if you compare with `equals`.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) on average, space O(n).
guide.pitfalls:
- `HashSet` loses the order; `TreeSet` sorts.
- `o == v` on `Integer` objects compares references and fails above 127.
- Removing from the input list, which may be unmodifiable.

java-code-word-count.title: Word frequencies with a HashMap
java-code-word-count.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static Map<String, Integer> wordCount(String text)
```

Split `text` into words at runs of spaces, convert each word to lower case, and return a map from each word
to the number of times it occurs. Leading and trailing spaces are ignored. An empty or all-space text gives
an empty map.

**Example** `wordCount("To be or not to be")` → `{to=2, be=2, or=1, not=1}` (the order of a map's entries
does not matter).

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Collections: List, Set, Map and Queue*: the counting idiom with `merge`.
guide.intuition: A map from word to count. For each word: if it is new, store 1; otherwise add 1 to what is there. `merge` does both in one call.
hints: `text.trim().split(" +")` gives the words; skip an empty string.
`counts.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum)` inserts 1 or adds 1.
Lower-case the word before using it as the key.
guide.brute_force: `if (counts.containsKey(w)) counts.put(w, counts.get(w) + 1); else counts.put(w, 1);` is the long form of the same thing, with two lookups.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) in the length of the text, space O(distinct words).
guide.pitfalls:
- `put(word, 1)` overwrites instead of counting.
- Forgetting to lower-case.
- `split(" ")` produces empty words for double spaces, and `"".split(...)` yields one empty string.

java-code-common-elements.title: Common elements with a HashSet
java-code-common-elements.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static List<Integer> common(int[] a, int[] b)
```

Return the values that occur in **both** arrays, each once, in **ascending** order.

**Examples** `common({4, 9, 5, 4}, {9, 4, 9, 8})` → `[4, 9]`; `common({1, 2}, {3})` → `[]`.

Aim for time proportional to the total length (plus sorting the answer), not `a.length × b.length`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Collections: List, Set, Map and Queue*: `HashSet` for fast membership tests, `TreeSet` for sorted results.
guide.intuition: Put one array into a hash set so that 'is this value in it?' takes constant time. Walk the other array and keep the hits in a set that sorts.
hints: Fill a `HashSet<Integer>` from `a`.
For each element of `b` that the set contains, add it to a `TreeSet`.
Return `new ArrayList<>(treeSet)`.
guide.brute_force: Compare every element of `a` with every element of `b`: O(a × b), and you must still remove duplicates and sort.
guide.complexity: Time O(a + b + k log k) for k common values, space O(a + k).
guide.pitfalls:
- Nested loops produce duplicates and quadratic time.
- Forgetting to sort the result.
- `list.contains` inside the loop makes it quadratic again.

java-code-valid-parentheses.title: Valid parentheses
java-code-valid-parentheses.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static boolean isValid(String s)
```

`s` contains only the characters `( ) [ ] { }`. It is valid when every opening bracket is closed by the same
kind of bracket, and brackets close in the correct order. The empty string is valid.

**Examples** `isValid("()[]{}")` → `true`; `isValid("([)]")` → `false`; `isValid("{[]}")` → `true`;
`isValid("(")` → `false`.

Use a `Deque` as a stack (`ArrayDeque`), not the legacy `Stack` class.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Collections: List, Set, Map and Queue*: `Deque` used as a stack (`push`, `pop`, `isEmpty`).
guide.intuition: The most recently opened bracket must be the first one closed. 'Last in, first out' is a stack.
hints: Push every opening bracket.
On a closing bracket: an empty stack means there is nothing to close; otherwise pop and check that the kinds match.
At the end the stack must be empty.
guide.brute_force: Repeatedly delete the substrings `()`, `[]` and `{}` until nothing changes; the string is valid if it becomes empty. Correct, and O(n²).
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n).
guide.pitfalls:
- Counting instead of stacking.
- Popping an empty stack (`NoSuchElementException`).
- Returning `true` without checking that the stack is empty.

java-code-top-k.title: K largest with a PriorityQueue
java-code-top-k.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static List<Integer> topK(int[] values, int k)
```

Return the `k` largest elements in **descending** order. Duplicates count separately. If `k` is larger than
the array, return all elements (still descending). `k >= 0`.

**Examples** `topK({5, 1, 9, 3, 9}, 3)` → `[9, 9, 5]`; `topK({4, 2}, 5)` → `[4, 2]`; `topK({1}, 0)` → `[]`.

Solve it with a `PriorityQueue` that never holds more than `k` elements, so the work is proportional to
n log k and not n log n.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Collections: List, Set, Map and Queue* (`PriorityQueue`) and *Sorting with Comparable and Comparator*.
guide.intuition: Keep a small 'leader board' of the k best values seen so far. The value you most often need from it is the **weakest** leader, to compare with a newcomer, so the board is a **min**-heap.
hints: A default `PriorityQueue<Integer>` hands out the smallest element first.
After each insertion, if the heap holds more than `k` elements, remove the smallest.
Iterating over a heap is not sorted: sort the survivors in reverse order at the end.
guide.brute_force: Sort the whole array in descending order and take the first k: O(n log n). Fine for small inputs; the heap wins when k is much smaller than n.
guide.complexity: Time O(n log k + k log k), space O(k).
guide.pitfalls:
- A max-heap capped at k keeps the k **smallest**.
- Returning the heap's iteration order, which is not sorted.
- Forgetting `k = 0`.

java-code-generic-largest.title: A generic method with a bound
java-code-generic-largest.description:
In class `Solution`, write a **generic** method that works for any type with a natural ordering:

```java
static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T largest(List<? extends T> items)
```

Return the largest element according to `compareTo`. If several elements are equally large, return the
first of them. For an empty list throw `java.util.NoSuchElementException`.

It must work for `List<Integer>`, `List<String>`, `List<java.time.LocalDate>` and so on, with no casts in
the calling code.

**Examples** `largest(List.of(4, 19, 7))` → `19`; `largest(List.of("pear", "fig", "plum"))` → `"plum"`.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Generics, wildcards and bounds* and *Bounded wildcards, PECS, varargs and heterogeneous containers*.
guide.intuition: The type parameter `T` stands for whatever the caller's list holds. The bound `Comparable<? super T>` is what entitles the method body to call `compareTo` on a `T`.
hints: Read the signature aloud: any `T` that can be compared with `T` or a supertype of `T`.
The list is a producer of `T`s, hence `List<? extends T>`.
Keep the first element as `best` and replace it only when `item.compareTo(best) > 0`.
guide.brute_force: `Collections.max(items)` does exactly this in the library, with the same signature shape. Writing it by hand shows why the bound is needed.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Returning `null` for an empty list instead of throwing.
- `>=`, which returns the last of several equal elements.
- Declaring the parameter as `List<Object>` and casting.

java-code-stream-names.title: A stream pipeline: filter, map, distinct, sorted
java-code-stream-names.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static List<String> longNames(List<String> names, int minLength)
```

Using a **stream pipeline**, return the names whose length (after trimming spaces at both ends) is at least
`minLength`, converted to upper case, without duplicates, sorted alphabetically.

**Example** `longNames(List.of("ada", " Grace ", "bo", "grace", "Linus"), 4)` → `["GRACE", "LINUS"]`.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Lambdas, functional interfaces and method references* and *The Stream API, collectors and Optional*.
guide.intuition: Describe the result as a series of stations: trim, keep the long ones, upper-case, drop duplicates, sort, collect.
hints: Start with `names.stream()`.
Order matters: trim before measuring the length, and upper-case before `distinct()` so that `grace` and `Grace` merge.
Finish with `.toList()`.
guide.brute_force: A loop with a `TreeSet<String>`: trim, test, upper-case, add; then copy the set to a list. The same result in more lines.
guide.complexity: Time O(n log n) because of the sort, space O(n).
guide.pitfalls:
- Filtering before trimming.
- `distinct()` before upper-casing leaves `Tea` and `tea` as two entries.
- `>` instead of `>=`.
- Forgetting the terminal operation: nothing runs.

java-code-count-by-length.title: Grouping with collectors
java-code-count-by-length.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static Map<Integer, Long> countByLength(List<String> words)
static Map<Boolean, List<String>> splitByVowelStart(List<String> words)
```

- `countByLength` returns, for each word length that occurs, how many words have that length.
- `splitByVowelStart` returns a map with exactly the two keys `true` and `false`: `true` → the words that
  start with a vowel (`a e i o u`, either case), `false` → the others; each list keeps the original order.
  Words are never empty.

Use `Collectors.groupingBy` with `Collectors.counting()`, and `Collectors.partitioningBy`.

**Examples** `countByLength(List.of("tea", "jam", "scone"))` → `{3=2, 5=1}`;
`splitByVowelStart(List.of("apple", "tea", "Oat"))` → `{true=[apple, Oat], false=[tea]}`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *The Stream API, collectors and Optional*: `groupingBy`, downstream collectors and `partitioningBy`.
guide.intuition: `groupingBy(key, counting())` is the stream form of the counting loop. `partitioningBy(test)` is a grouping with a boolean key that always produces both keys.
hints: The classifier for the first method is `String::length`.
`Collectors.counting()` yields `Long` values.
Use `partitioningBy`, not `groupingBy`, when both `true` and `false` must be present even if one list is empty.
guide.brute_force: Two ordinary loops with `merge` and `computeIfAbsent` do the same and are perfectly good Java. The collectors say it in one expression.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(n).
guide.pitfalls:
- `groupingBy` with a boolean classifier omits a key that has no elements.
- Forgetting upper-case vowels.
- Expecting `Integer` counts: `counting()` produces `Long`.

java-code-compose-functions.title: Lambdas: build a pipeline of functions
java-code-compose-functions.description:
Functions are values. In class `Solution`, write

```java
static Function<Integer, Integer> pipeline(List<Function<Integer, Integer>> steps)
static Predicate<Integer> allOf(List<Predicate<Integer>> tests)
```

- `pipeline` returns one function that applies the steps **in list order**: for steps `[f, g, h]` the result
  computes `h(g(f(x)))`. An empty list gives the identity function.
- `allOf` returns a predicate that is true when **every** test in the list is true. An empty list gives a
  predicate that is always true. It should stop at the first failing test.

**Example**

```java
Function<Integer, Integer> p = Solution.pipeline(List.of(x -> x + 1, x -> x * 10));
p.apply(4);     // 50
```

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Lambdas, functional interfaces and method references* and *Choosing between lambdas, method references and classes*.
guide.intuition: Start from a function that does nothing and chain each step onto the end with `andThen`. The same folding idea works for predicates with `and`.
hints: `Function.identity()` returns its argument unchanged.
`f.andThen(g)` runs `f` first and then `g`; `compose` is the reverse order.
`Predicate.and` short-circuits: if the left side is false, the right side is not evaluated.
guide.brute_force: Return a lambda that loops over the list each time it is called: `x -> { for (var s : steps) x = s.apply(x); return x; }`. Just as valid, and arguably clearer; note that it captures the list, so later changes to the list would show through.
guide.complexity: Building is O(k) for k steps; each call of the result is O(k).
guide.pitfalls:
- `compose` applies the steps in reverse.
- `allOf` of an empty list must be true, not false.
- Using `|` or evaluating every test defeats short-circuiting.

java-code-record-range.title: A record with validation
java-code-record-range.description:
Inside `Solution`, write a **record** for a closed range of whole numbers.

```java
record Range(int lo, int hi) {
    // compact constructor: throw IllegalArgumentException if lo > hi
    int length()                     // number of integers in the range: hi - lo + 1
    boolean contains(int value)      // lo <= value <= hi
    boolean overlaps(Range other)    // do the two ranges share at least one integer?
    static Range of(int a, int b)    // factory that accepts the bounds in either order
}
```

A record gives you the accessors `lo()` and `hi()`, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString` automatically:
`new Range(1, 5).toString()` is `"Range[lo=1, hi=5]"`.

**Examples** `new Range(3, 7).length()` → `5`; `Range.of(9, 2)` equals `new Range(2, 9)`;
`new Range(5, 1)` throws `IllegalArgumentException`.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Classes and objects: blueprint and building* (records), *Constructors, this and super* (compact constructors).
guide.intuition: A record is a class whose state is exactly its components. You add the rule (lo ≤ hi) in the compact constructor, and behaviour as ordinary methods; equality and printing come for free.
hints: A compact constructor has no parameter list: `Range { ... }`. The fields are assigned automatically after your checks.
Two closed ranges overlap when each starts no later than the other ends.
`of` normalises the order with `Math.min` and `Math.max`.
guide.brute_force: A hand-written class needs a constructor, two private final fields, two accessors, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`: about thirty lines to say what `record Range(int lo, int hi)` says.
guide.complexity: Every operation is O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- No validation: an invalid `Range(5, 1)` can then exist.
- `hi - lo` for the length (off by one).
- Strict `<` in `contains` or `overlaps` excludes the end points of a closed range.

java-code-money-equals.title: equals and hashCode by hand

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Writing equals and hashCode correctly*.
guide.intuition: `equals` answers 'same value?' field by field; `hashCode` must be computed from the same fields so that equal objects land in the same bucket.
hints: The parameter of `equals` must be `Object`; `@Override` makes the compiler check it.
`o instanceof Money other` handles both the type test and `null`.
Compare the `long` with `==` and the `String` with `equals`; combine their hashes with the multiplier 31.
guide.brute_force: A record generates all three methods: `record Money(long cents, String currency) { }`. Writing them by hand once shows what the record is doing for you.
guide.complexity: Both methods are O(length of the currency string); effectively O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- `equals(Money other)` overloads instead of overriding: collections never call it.
- Overriding `equals` without `hashCode`: hash collections treat equal objects as different.
- Comparing the `String` field with `==`.
- A constant `hashCode` is legal and makes every hash table a linked list.

java-code-immutable-playlist.title: An immutable class with defensive copies
java-code-immutable-playlist.description:
Inside `Solution`, write an **immutable** class.

```java
static final class Playlist {
    Playlist(String name, List<String> tracks)      // NullPointerException if name or tracks is null
    String name()
    List<String> tracks()                           // the tracks, in order
    int size()
    Playlist withTrack(String track)                // a NEW playlist with the track added at the end; this one is unchanged
}
```

Nothing outside the class may be able to change a playlist after it is created:

- changing the list passed to the constructor afterwards must not affect the playlist;
- changing the list returned by `tracks()` must not affect the playlist. (It is fine for that list to throw
  `UnsupportedOperationException` on modification, or to be a copy.)

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Minimal accessibility and immutable classes* and *Parameter checks, defensive copies, signatures and overloading*.
guide.intuition: `private final` fields are not enough when a field refers to a mutable list: the caller still holds the list they passed in, and a getter hands the list out again. Copy on the way in, and return something that cannot be modified.
hints: `List.copyOf(tracks)` makes an independent, unmodifiable copy and throws `NullPointerException` for a null list.
An unmodifiable list can be returned directly from `tracks()`.
`withTrack` builds a new list and a new `Playlist`; it never touches `this`.
guide.brute_force: `Collections.unmodifiableList(tracks)` around the caller's own list protects the getter and still leaves the constructor's back door open: the view shows every later change to the original.
guide.complexity: Construction and `withTrack` are O(n) for n tracks; the accessors are O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Storing the caller's list.
- Returning the internal mutable list.
- `withTrack` that modifies `this`.
- Wrapping without copying.

java-code-builder.title: The builder pattern
java-code-builder.description:
Inside `Solution`, implement a class with a **builder**.

```java
static final class Pizza {
    static Builder builder(int sizeCm)          // the size is required
    int sizeCm()
    String crust()                              // default "classic"
    boolean extraCheese()                       // default false
    List<String> toppings()                     // default empty; in the order added

    static final class Builder {
        Builder crust(String crust)             // returns this
        Builder extraCheese()                   // returns this
        Builder topping(String topping)         // returns this
        Pizza build()                           // validates, then creates the Pizza
    }
}
```

`build()` throws `IllegalStateException` if the size is not between 15 and 50 (inclusive) or if there are
more than 5 toppings. The built `Pizza` must not change if the builder is used again afterwards.

**Example**

```java
Pizza p = Pizza.builder(30).crust("thin").topping("olive").extraCheese().build();
p.crust();        // "thin"
p.toppings();     // [olive]
```

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Static factories, builders, singletons and dependency injection*.
guide.intuition: Two classes share the work. The builder is a mutable scratch pad whose methods return `this` so calls can be chained. `build()` checks the rules once and hands the values to a private constructor of the immutable product.
hints: Give the builder its own fields with default values.
Every configuration method ends with `return this;`.
In the `Pizza` constructor copy the toppings (`List.copyOf`) so the builder and the pizza no longer share a list.
guide.brute_force: A constructor `Pizza(int, String, boolean, List<String>)` works for four parameters and becomes unreadable at eight: `new Pizza(30, "thin", true, false, true, null)`.
guide.complexity: Each builder call is O(1); `build()` is O(number of toppings).
guide.pitfalls:
- Sharing the builder's list with the built object.
- Forgetting `return this`.
- Validating with the wrong boundaries (15 and 50 are allowed).
- No validation of the topping count.

java-code-two-sum.title: Two Sum in Java
java-code-two-sum.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target)
```

Return the indices `{i, j}` with `i < j` of the two different positions whose values add up to `target`.
Exactly one such pair exists.

**Examples** `twoSum({2, 7, 11, 15}, 9)` → `{0, 1}`; `twoSum({3, 2, 4}, 6)` → `{1, 2}`; `twoSum({3, 3}, 6)` → `{0, 1}`.

Solve it in one pass with a `HashMap`; arrays may have 100,000 elements.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Collections: List, Set, Map and Queue*: `HashMap` lookups in constant time.
guide.intuition: For each number, the partner it needs is `target - number`. Remember every number already seen, with its index, and ask the map whether the partner has appeared.
hints: Map from value to index.
Look up the partner **before** storing the current number, so an element is never paired with itself.
The stored index is the smaller one: return `{stored, current}`.
guide.brute_force: Two nested loops over all pairs `i < j`: O(n²). With 100,000 elements that is five billion additions.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) on average, space O(n).
guide.pitfalls:
- Pairing an element with itself (`{0, 0}` for `{3, 2, 4}` and target 6).
- Unboxing a `null` from `map.get`.
- Filling the whole map first and then finding the same index twice.

java-code-binary-search.title: Binary search in Java
java-code-binary-search.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static int search(int[] sorted, int target)
```

`sorted` is in ascending order with no duplicates. Return the index of `target`, or `-1` if it is absent.
The method must run in logarithmic time: arrays may hold a million elements and the test checks many
lookups.

**Examples** `search({-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12}, 9)` → `4`; `search({-1, 0, 3, 5, 9, 12}, 2)` → `-1`.

Take care with the middle index: `(lo + hi) / 2` can overflow an `int` for very large arrays.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Loops, operators and casting* and *Primitive types and how numbers are stored* (overflow).
guide.intuition: Because the array is sorted, one comparison with the middle element rules out half of what is left. Keep the bounds of the part still under suspicion and halve it until it is empty.
hints: `lo` and `hi` are inclusive bounds of the remaining range.
The loop runs while `lo <= hi`; with `<` a single remaining element is never examined.
Compute `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2` and compare with `<`, never by subtracting.
guide.brute_force: Scan from the left until you meet the target: O(n). The million-element test with 300,000 lookups would take far too long.
guide.complexity: Time O(log n), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- `while (lo < hi)` skips the last candidate.
- Not moving past `mid` (`lo = mid`) can loop for ever.
- Comparing with `sorted[mid] - target < 0` overflows for values of opposite sign.

java-code-reverse-linked-list.title: Reverse a linked list in Java

guide.prereqs: Lesson *References, arrays, the stack and the heap*: objects that refer to each other; re-pointing references.
guide.intuition: Walk along the list turning each arrow round. Before overwriting a node's `next`, save it, or the rest of the list is lost.
hints: Three references: `previous` (starts `null`), `current` (starts at the head) and a saved `next`.
Inside the loop: save, re-point, advance both.
When `current` becomes `null`, `previous` is the new head.
guide.brute_force: Copy the values into an `ArrayList`, then build a new list backwards. O(n) extra memory and new nodes, which the task forbids.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Overwriting `current.next` before saving it.
- Stopping one node early and returning the wrong head.
- A recursive version overflows the stack on a list of 20,000 nodes.

java-code-merge-intervals.title: Merge intervals in Java
java-code-merge-intervals.description:
In class `Solution`, write

```java
static int[][] merge(int[][] intervals)
```

Each element of `intervals` is `{start, end}` with `start <= end`. Merge all intervals that overlap or
touch (`{1, 4}` and `{4, 5}` merge) and return the result sorted by start. The input is in no particular
order. Do not modify the arrays you were given.

**Examples** `merge({{1,3},{2,6},{8,10},{15,18}})` → `{{1,6},{8,10},{15,18}}`; `merge({{1,4},{4,5}})` → `{{1,5}}`.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Sorting with Comparable and Comparator* and *Collections: List, Set, Map and Queue*.
guide.intuition: Once the intervals are sorted by start, anything that overlaps the interval you are building must come next. So one pass suffices: extend the last result, or start a new one.
hints: Copy, then sort by `a[0]` with `Comparator.comparingInt`.
The current interval overlaps the last result when `last[1] >= cur[0]`.
When merging, the new end is the **maximum** of the two ends.
guide.brute_force: Compare every pair and merge until nothing changes: O(n²) or worse.
guide.complexity: Time O(n log n) for the sort, space O(n).
guide.pitfalls:
- Forgetting to sort.
- Setting the end to `cur[1]` when the current interval lies inside the last one.
- `<=` versus `<`: touching intervals merge.
- Sorting or editing the caller's arrays.

java-code-lru-cache.title: LRU cache in Java

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Collections: List, Set, Map and Queue* (`LinkedHashMap`), *Needless objects, memory leaks and resource clean-up* (bounded caches), *Nested, inner, local and anonymous classes*.
guide.intuition: Two needs at once: find a key instantly (a hash map) and know which key was used longest ago (an ordering by recency). `LinkedHashMap` in **access order** maintains exactly that ordering, and calls `removeEldestEntry` after every insertion.
hints: `new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true)`: the third argument switches from insertion order to access order.
Override `removeEldestEntry` to return `size() > capacity`.
`get` must go through the map's own `get` so that the access is recorded; translate `null` to -1.
guide.brute_force: A plain `LinkedHashMap` in insertion order evicts the oldest **inserted** key, which is FIFO, not LRU: a `get` does not refresh a key. Tracking recency in an `ArrayList` works and makes every operation O(n).
guide.complexity: Time O(1) average for both operations, space O(capacity).
guide.pitfalls:
- Insertion order instead of access order.
- Refusing new keys when full, instead of evicting.
- Forgetting that updating an existing key also refreshes it.
- Unboxing a `null` result.

java-int-arithmetic.title: int and long arithmetic: overflow and integer division
java-int-arithmetic.description:
Java's `int` has 32 bits and `long` has 64. Results that do not fit **wrap around** silently, division of
whole numbers **truncates toward zero**, and `%` takes the **sign of the left operand**. Python's integers
do none of these things, so you must model them.

Write `java_arith(kind, a, op, b)`.

- `kind` is `"int"` or `"long"`. `a` and `b` are already valid values of that type.
- `op` is one of `"+"`, `"-"`, `"*"`, `"/"`, `"%"`.
- Return the value Java would compute, as a Python integer.
- For `"/"` or `"%"` with `b == 0`, return the string `"ArithmeticException"`.

**Wrapping rule** for a type with `n` bits: keep the true result modulo `2^n`; if that is `>= 2^(n-1)`,
subtract `2^n`.

**Examples**

- `java_arith("int", 2147483647, "+", 1)` → `-2147483648`
- `java_arith("int", -7, "/", 2)` → `-3` (Python's `//` would give `-4`)
- `java_arith("int", -7, "%", 2)` → `-1` (Python's `%` would give `1`)

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Primitive types and how numbers are stored*: bits, ranges, integer division, overflow.
guide.intuition: Python never overflows and rounds division downward. Compute the exact mathematical result first, fix division so it rounds toward zero, then squeeze the result back into 32 or 64 bits.
hints: Handle division by zero before anything else.
Truncating division: divide the absolute values, then put the sign back. The remainder is `a - q * b`.
To wrap: `v & (2**bits - 1)` keeps the low bits; if the top bit is set, subtract `2**bits`.
guide.brute_force: You could special-case every overflow direction with `if` statements. It works for `+` and `-` and becomes hopeless for `*`. Masking handles all three with one line.
guide.approach:
1. If the operator is `/` or `%` and `b` is 0, return `"ArithmeticException"`.
2. Compute the exact result with Python's unlimited integers. For `/`, use `q = abs(a) // abs(b)` and negate
   `q` if the signs differ. For `%`, use `a - q * b`.
3. Wrap: mask to the low `bits` bits, and reinterpret the top bit as the sign.

**Dry run** `java_arith("int", 86400000, "*", 30)`: exact product `2592000000`. It is below `2^32`, so the
mask leaves it alone. It is `>= 2^31` (2147483648), so subtract `2^32`: `2592000000 - 4294967296 = -1702967296`.

**Dry run** `java_arith("int", -2147483648, "/", -1)`: `q = 2147483648`, signs equal so it stays positive;
that does not fit, and wrapping gives `-2147483648`. Java really does print that.

```java
int big = Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1;            // -2147483648: wraps silently
int q = -7 / 2;                             // -3: truncates toward zero
int r = -7 % 2;                             // -1: sign of the left operand
long ok = 86_400_000L * 30;                 // 2592000000: one long operand makes it 64-bit
int safe = Math.addExact(big, 1);           // throws ArithmeticException on overflow instead of wrapping
```
guide.complexity: Time O(1), space O(1): a fixed number of arithmetic steps.
guide.pitfalls:
- Using Python's `//` and `%`, which round toward negative infinity.
- Forgetting that `Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1` overflows.
- Wrapping with `% 2**bits` only: that gives a value from 0 upward and never a negative one.
guide.follow_up: Add the shifts `<<`, `>>` and `>>>`. In Java the shift distance is itself masked to 5 bits for `int` and 6 for `long`.

java-char-string-concat.title: What does + mean? char, int and String
java-char-string-concat.description:
In Java `+` is evaluated **left to right**, and its meaning depends on the two operands at each step:

- if **either** operand is a `String`, it is concatenation and the result is a `String`
  (an `int` is appended as decimal digits, a `char` as the character itself);
- otherwise it is numeric addition and the result is an `int` (a `char` contributes its character code).

Write `plus_chain(terms)`. Each term is a pair `[type, value]`:

- `["int", 5]`
- `["char", "a"]` (a one-character string)
- `["String", "hi"]`

Evaluate `term0 + term1 + term2 + ...` and return the result as `[type, value]`: either `["int", n]` or
`["String", text]`. A single `char` term with nothing added stays a `char`: return it unchanged.
`terms` is never empty. Ignore overflow.

**Examples**

- `'a' + 'b'` → `["int", 195]`
- `1 + 2 + "3"` → `["String", "33"]`
- `"" + 'a' + 1` → `["String", "a1"]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Primitive types and how numbers are stored*: `char` is a number, and the left-to-right rule for `+`.
guide.intuition: Keep one running result with its type. Each new term either gets added as a number or glued on as text, and the decision depends only on the running type and the new term's type.
hints: Start with the first term as the running value.
At each step ask: is the running value a String, or is the new term a String? Then concatenate.
Otherwise convert any `char` to its code with `ord` and add; the result type is `int`.
guide.brute_force: Checking 'is there a String anywhere?' and concatenating everything is the common wrong idea: it ignores that the terms **before** the first String are added as numbers.
guide.approach:
Fold from the left.

**Dry run** `'a' + 'b' + "c" + 'd' + 1`:

| step | running | next | rule | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | char `a` | char `b` | no String: numeric | int 195 |
| 2 | int 195 | String `c` | String: append | String `195c` |
| 3 | String `195c` | char `d` | String: append the character | String `195cd` |
| 4 | String `195cd` | int 1 | String: append digits | String `195cd1` |

```java
System.out.println('a' + 'b');             // 195
System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3");           // 33
System.out.println("" + 'a' + 1);          // a1
System.out.println('a' + 'b' + "c" + 'd' + 1);   // 195cd1
char next = (char) ('a' + 1);              // 'b': cast the int back to a char
```
guide.complexity: Time O(total length of the result), space the same: one pass over the terms.
guide.pitfalls:
- Treating the whole expression as concatenation because a String appears somewhere.
- Appending a `char`'s numeric code to a String; Java appends the character.
- Returning `["int", 120]` for a lone `char`: with nothing added there is no promotion.

java-switch-fallthrough.title: Classic switch: fall-through
java-switch-fallthrough.description:
A classic Java `switch` (the form with colons) jumps to the matching `case` label and then keeps running
**downward through the following cases** until it meets a `break` or the end of the switch.

Write `run_switch(value, cases)` that returns the list of texts printed.

- `cases` is a list, in source order, of `[label, text, has_break]`.
- `label` is an integer, or `None` for the `default` label (at most one, anywhere in the list).
- Entry point: the case whose label equals `value`; if there is none, the `default` case; if there is no
  default either, nothing is printed.
- From the entry point, print each case's `text` in order, stopping after the first case whose `has_break`
  is true.

**Example**

```
switch (2) { case 3: print("three"); case 2: print("two"); case 1: print("one"); break; default: print("other"); }
```
`run_switch(2, [[3, "three", False], [2, "two", False], [1, "one", True], [None, "other", False]])` → `["two", "one"]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Anatomy of a class, main, and your first statements*: the classic and the arrow form of `switch`.
guide.intuition: Two separate questions: **where do I enter**, and **where do I stop**. Entry is decided once. After that the labels no longer matter; only `break` does.
hints: First search for a label equal to the value.
Only if that fails, search for the default.
From the entry index, collect texts until you have collected one that has a break.
guide.brute_force: Returning only the matching case's text is how an arrow switch behaves. For the classic form it is wrong whenever a `break` is missing.
guide.complexity: Time O(n) in the number of cases, space O(n) for the output.
guide.pitfalls:
- Entering at the default because it appears before the matching case in the source.
- Stopping at the default.
- Forgetting the switch with no match and no default.

java-array-defaults-bounds.title: Arrays: default values and bounds checks
java-array-defaults-bounds.description:
`new int[4]` creates four slots that already hold a **default value**, and every access is **bounds-checked**.

Write `array_ops(elem_type, length, ops)` simulating `new elem_type[length]` followed by operations.

- `elem_type` is `"int"`, `"double"`, `"boolean"`, `"char"` or `"String"`.
- Defaults: `0`, `0.0`, `False`, `"\u0000"` (the character with code 0) and `None` (Java's `null`).
- If `length` is negative, return `["NegativeArraySizeException: " + str(length)]` and do nothing else.
- `ops` is a list of:
  - `["get", i]` → append the element at index `i` to the output;
  - `["set", i, v]` → store `v` (append nothing);
  - `["length"]` → append the length.
- An index below 0 or at or above the length ends the run: append
  `"ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index <i> out of bounds for length <n>"` and stop.

Return the output list.

**Example** `array_ops("int", 3, [["get", 1], ["set", 1, 9], ["get", 1], ["get", 3], ["length"]])`
→ `[0, 9, "ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 3 out of bounds for length 3"]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *References, arrays, the stack and the heap*: arrays are objects with zero-based indices.
guide.intuition: A Java array is a fixed row of slots pre-filled with the type's zero value. Python lists accept negative indices, so the bounds check has to be written by hand.
hints: Deal with a negative length first.
Build the array as `[default] * length` using a table of defaults.
Check `0 <= i < length` before every get and set; on failure append the message and stop.
guide.brute_force: Without the explicit check, `arr[-1]` in Python quietly reads the last element. Java would throw.
guide.complexity: Time O(length + number of operations), space O(length).
guide.pitfalls:
- `None` as the default for every type.
- Allowing Python's negative indices.
- Continuing after an exception.
- `i > length` instead of `i >= length`.

expected: ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 3 out of bounds for length 3
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 0 out of bounds for length 0
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index -1 out of bounds for length 4
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 4 out of bounds for length 4
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException: Index 2 out of bounds for length 2

java-reference-model.title: References, aliases and pass-by-value
java-reference-model.description:
Model a tiny Java program working with `class Box { int v; }`. Variables hold **references** to boxes
(or `null`). Assignment copies the reference. Arguments are passed **by value**: a method gets a copy of
the reference.

Write `run_program(ops)`; each op is one statement:

| op | Java | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `["new", x, n]` | `Box x = new Box(); x.v = n;` | `x` refers to a new box |
| `["assign", x, y]` | `x = y;` | `x` refers to whatever `y` refers to (maybe `null`) |
| `["null", x]` | `x = null;` | |
| `["set", x, n]` | `x.v = n;` | |
| `["mutate", x, n]` | `mutate(x, n)` where `static void mutate(Box b, int n) { b.v = n; }` | changes the caller's box |
| `["reassign", x, n]` | `reassign(x, n)` where `static void reassign(Box b, int n) { b = new Box(); b.v = n; }` | **no effect on the caller** |
| `["swap", x, y]` | `swap(x, y)` where the method exchanges its two parameters | **no effect on the caller** |
| `["print", x]` | `System.out.println(x.v);` | append the value to the output |
| `["same", x, y]` | `System.out.println(x == y);` | append `True` or `False` |

`set`, `mutate` and `print` on a variable holding `null` throw: append `"NullPointerException"` and stop.
(`reassign`, `swap` and `same` work with `null`.) Every variable used has been created earlier by `new`,
`assign` or `null`. Return the output list.

**Example** `[["new","a",1], ["assign","b","a"], ["set","b",5], ["print","a"], ["reassign","a",9], ["print","a"], ["same","a","b"]]`
→ `[5, 5, True]`

guide.prereqs: Lessons *References, arrays, the stack and the heap* and *Methods, parameters, return values and pass-by-value*.
guide.intuition: Keep two tables: a **frame** mapping variable names to object ids (or `None`), and a **heap** mapping object ids to the box's value. Assignment copies an id. A method receives copies of ids, so it can change the heap but never the caller's frame.
hints: Give every `new` a fresh object id.
`same` compares ids, not values.
`reassign` and `swap` change only the method's own copies: the caller's frame is untouched.
guide.brute_force: Storing the number directly in the variable (no heap) cannot represent two variables sharing one box, so aliasing is lost.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** of the example. `new a 1`: heap `{#1: 1}`, frame `{a: #1}`. `assign b a`: frame
`{a: #1, b: #1}`. `set b 5`: heap `{#1: 5}`. `print a` → 5 (same box). `reassign a 9`: the method's local
copy points at a new box #2, which becomes garbage; frame unchanged. `print a` → 5. `same a b` → True.

```java
class Box { int v; }

static void mutate(Box b, int n)   { b.v = n; }                    // follows the copied reference
static void reassign(Box b, int n) { b = new Box(); b.v = n; }     // re-points only the local copy
static void swap(Box x, Box y)     { Box t = x; x = y; y = t; }    // swaps only the local copies

Box a = new Box();  a.v = 1;
Box b = a;                       // alias
b.v = 5;                         // a.v is 5 too
reassign(a, 9);                  // a.v is still 5
System.out.println(a == b);      // true: same object
```
guide.complexity: Time O(number of statements), space O(number of boxes created).
guide.pitfalls:
- Comparing values for `==`.
- Letting `reassign` or `swap` change the caller's variables.
- Throwing for `same` on `null`: comparing references with `==` never throws.

java-casting-narrowing.title: Narrowing casts
java-casting-narrowing.description:
A cast such as `(byte) x` or `(int) d` may lose information. Model the two rules.

Write `narrow(value, target)` where `target` is `"byte"`, `"short"`, `"char"`, `"int"` or `"long"`.

**Whole-number source** (`value` is a Python `int` that fits in a Java `long`): keep the low
8 / 16 / 16 / 32 / 64 bits. `byte`, `short`, `int` and `long` are signed (reinterpret the top bit as a sign);
`char` is **unsigned** (0 to 65535).

**Fractional source** (`value` is a Python `float`, standing for a Java `double`):

1. Drop the fraction (round toward zero).
2. If the target is `long`: clamp to the `long` range. Otherwise clamp to the **`int`** range first, and then
   apply the whole-number rule to reach `byte`, `short` or `char`.

Return a Python `int`.

**Examples** `narrow(300, "byte")` → `44`; `narrow(-1, "char")` → `65535`; `narrow(3.99, "int")` → `3`;
`narrow(-3.99, "int")` → `-3`; `narrow(1e20, "int")` → `2147483647`.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Primitive types and how numbers are stored* and *Loops, operators and casting*.
guide.intuition: Integer narrowing throws away high bits. Floating-point narrowing first becomes a clamped `int` or `long`, then, for small targets, throws away high bits as well.
hints: `int(x)` on a Python float truncates toward zero, which is what Java does.
Clamp a truncated float to the int range (or the long range when the target is long).
Mask to the target's bit count; subtract `2**bits` if the top bit is set, except for `char`.
guide.brute_force: Rounding with `round()` is the usual mistake: `(int) 3.99` is 3, not 4.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** `narrow(1e10, "byte")`: truncate → 10000000000. Target is not long, so clamp to the int
range → 2147483647, which is `0x7FFFFFFF`. Low 8 bits are `0xFF` = 255; the top bit is set, so 255 - 256 = `-1`.
Java prints `-1` for `(byte) 1e10`.

```java
System.out.println((byte) 300);          // 44
System.out.println((int) (char) -1);     // 65535
System.out.println((int) 3.99);          // 3
System.out.println((int) -3.99);         // -3
System.out.println((int) 1e20);          // 2147483647
System.out.println((byte) 1e10);         // -1
System.out.println(Math.round(3.99));    // 4: use round when you want rounding
```
guide.complexity: Time O(1), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Rounding instead of truncating.
- Treating `char` as signed.
- Masking a huge float directly to 8 bits without first clamping to the int range.

java-vault-feedback.title: Vault Dial feedback
java-vault-feedback.description:
The game from the lesson *Building a small game: the Vault Dial*. The vault holds a secret list of digits;
the player guesses a list of the same length. Return `[exact, near]`:

- `exact`: positions where the guess digit equals the secret digit;
- `near`: guess digits that are **not** exact but match a secret digit elsewhere. Each secret digit can be
  matched by **at most one** guess digit, and a secret digit used for an exact match cannot also be used
  for a near match.

Digits may repeat in either list. Lengths are equal (possibly zero).

**Examples** secret `[4, 7, 2]`:
`feedback([4,7,2], [2,7,9])` → `[1, 1]`; `feedback([4,7,2], [7,7,7])` → `[1, 0]`; `feedback([4,7,2], [2,4,7])` → `[0, 3]`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Building a small game: the Vault Dial*, where a test exposed the repeated-digit bug.
guide.intuition: Count exact matches first and set those positions aside. Among what is left, a digit can pair up as many times as it appears on **both** sides: the minimum of the two counts.
hints: Do the exact pass separately.
Tally the leftover secret digits and the leftover guess digits.
For each digit, near matches = `min(leftover in guess, leftover in secret)`.
guide.brute_force: For each non-exact guess digit, search the secret for an unused equal digit and mark it used: O(n²), and it is what the lesson's Java code does. Fine for three digits.
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(k) for k distinct digits.
guide.pitfalls:
- Counting a guess digit as near because the digit exists somewhere in the secret.
- Counting exact matches again in the near total.
guide.follow_up: This is the scoring rule of the classic game Bulls and Cows.

java-arraylist-growth.title: How ArrayList grows
java-arraylist-growth.description:
`java.util.ArrayList` stores its elements in an internal array. When an `add` finds the array full, it
allocates a bigger array and copies the elements across.

Model `n` calls to `add` on a new list. Write `grow(n, initial)`:

- `initial == -1` means `new ArrayList<>()`: the capacity starts at 0 and the **first** growth goes to **10**.
- otherwise `new ArrayList<>(initial)` with `initial >= 0`: the capacity starts at `initial`.
- Every other growth, when the list is full: `new = old + old // 2`, but at least `old + 1`.
- Growing copies every element currently stored.

Return `[final_capacity, number_of_growths, total_elements_copied]`.

**Examples** `grow(11, -1)` → `[15, 2, 10]` (0 → 10 copying 0 elements, then 10 → 15 copying 10);
`grow(3, 0)` → `[3, 3, 3]` (0 → 1 → 2 → 3).

guide.prereqs: Lesson *ArrayList and reading the API documentation*: size versus capacity, and growth by half.
guide.intuition: Simulate it literally: a size, a capacity, and a rule for what the capacity becomes when the two meet.
hints: Grow only when `size == capacity`, immediately before the add.
The default constructor allocates nothing until the first add.
`old // 2` is 0 for capacities 0 and 1, so the 'at least old + 1' rule matters.
guide.brute_force: A closed formula exists but is fiddly because of the integer division. Simulation is clear and fast.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** `grow(11, -1)`. Add 1: size 0 = cap 0, default → cap 10, copied 0, growths 1. Adds 2 to 10
fit. Add 11: size 10 = cap 10 → cap 15, copied 10, growths 2. Result `[15, 2, 10]`.

Capacities for the default list: 10, 15, 22, 33, 49, 73, 109, 163, 244, 366, 549, 823, 1234. A thousand adds
copy about 2,500 elements in total: a small constant amount per add, which is why `add` is called
**amortised constant time**.

```java
List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();          // capacity 0 until the first add, then 10
List<String> sized = new ArrayList<>(1_000);     // reserve up front: no growth for 1,000 adds
((ArrayList<String>) names).ensureCapacity(500); // grow once, now
((ArrayList<String>) names).trimToSize();        // shrink the array to the current size
```
guide.complexity: Time O(n), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Doubling: Java grows by half.
- Starting the default list at capacity 10 and missing the first growth.
- Forgetting `max(..., old + 1)`, which leaves a list created with capacity 0 or 1 stuck.

java-integer-cache.title: Integer cache puzzles: == and equals
java-integer-cache.description:
`==` on two `Integer` references compares **identity**. Autoboxing calls `Integer.valueOf`, which returns
**cached** objects for values from -128 to 127 and a new object otherwise. That makes `==` true for small
numbers and false for large ones.

Write `evaluate(decls, queries)`.

`decls` is a list of declarations, in order:

| declaration | Java |
|---|---|
| `[name, "int", n]` | `int name = n;` |
| `[name, "Integer", n]` | `Integer name = n;` (autoboxed) |
| `[name, "new", n]` | `Integer name = new Integer(n);` (always a new object) |
| `[name, "alias", other]` | `Integer name = other;` where `other` is an earlier `Integer` variable |

`queries` is a list of `["==", a, b]` or `["equals", a, b]`. Return a list of booleans.

- `==`: if **either** side is an `int`, the other is unboxed and the numbers are compared. If both are
  `Integer` references, the result is true only when they refer to the same object.
- `equals` (the left side is always an `Integer` variable): true when the values are equal. An `int` on
  the right is boxed first.

**Example** `evaluate([["a","Integer",127],["b","Integer",127],["c","Integer",128],["d","Integer",128]], [["==","a","b"],["==","c","d"],["equals","c","d"]])` → `[True, False, True]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Wrapper classes, autoboxing and formatting*: the three traps of autoboxing.
guide.intuition: Give each `Integer` variable an **identity** as well as a value. Autoboxed small values share one identity per value; everything else gets a fresh one; an alias copies the identity.
hints: Track `value[name]` and `ident[name]`; use `None` as the identity of a primitive.
If either side of `==` is primitive, compare values.
Otherwise compare identities. A variable compared with itself is always the same object.
guide.brute_force: Comparing values everywhere answers `equals` correctly and gets `==` wrong for large numbers and for `new`.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** `a = 128` (autoboxed, fresh object #1), `b = new Integer(128)` (#2), `c = b` (alias, #2).
`a == b`: #1 vs #2 → False. `b == c`: #2 vs #2 → True. `a.equals(c)`: 128 = 128 → True. `a == c` → False.

The tempting shortcut "both boxed: equal values and in the cache range" fails for `new Integer(5) == new Integer(5)`
(two objects) and for `a == a` with a large value (one object).

```java
Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println(a == b);          // true: same cached object
System.out.println(c == d);          // false: two objects
System.out.println(c.equals(d));     // true: compare values with equals
System.out.println(c == 128);        // true: c is unboxed
System.out.println(Integer.compare(c, d) == 0);   // true, and null-safe alternatives exist in Objects
```
guide.complexity: Time O(declarations + queries), space O(declarations).
guide.pitfalls:
- Forgetting that `new Integer` never uses the cache.
- Treating an alias as a new object.
- Applying the cache rule when one side is a primitive.

java-try-finally-flow.title: try / catch / finally: what comes out?
java-try-finally-flow.description:
Predict the outcome of one `try` statement inside a method.

Write `flow(try_block, catches, fin, tail)`.

An **outcome** is one of `["ok"]` (the block finishes normally), `["return", value]` or `["throw", type]`.

- `try_block` is an outcome.
- `catches` is a list of `[caught_type, outcome]`, in source order. If the try block throws `T`, the **first**
  catch whose `caught_type` is `T` or a supertype of `T` runs; its outcome replaces the pending one.
- `fin` is an outcome, or `None` when there is no `finally`. If present it **always runs**. If it returns or
  throws, that **replaces** whatever was pending (a pending return value or exception is discarded).
- If nothing returned or threw, the method goes on and returns `tail`.

Use this fixed hierarchy (child → parent):
`FileNotFoundException → IOException → Exception → Throwable`, `NullPointerException → RuntimeException → Exception`,
`IllegalStateException → RuntimeException`, `OutOfMemoryError → Error → Throwable`.

Return `[kind, value, trace]`: `kind` is `"return"` or `"throw"`, `value` the returned value or the exception
type, and `trace` the blocks executed in order, from `"try"`, `"catch:<caught_type>"`, `"finally"`.

**Example** `flow(["throw", "FileNotFoundException"], [["IOException", ["return", 2]]], ["ok"], 0)`
→ `["return", 2, ["try", "catch:IOException", "finally"]]`
java-try-finally-flow.starter:
def flow(try_block, catches, fin, tail):
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Exceptions: try, catch, finally, checked and unchecked*.
guide.intuition: Carry one **pending outcome** through three stations: the try block sets it, a matching catch may replace it, and `finally` runs last and replaces it only if `finally` itself returns or throws.
hints: A catch matches the thrown type or any of its supertypes; take the first match only.
`finally` runs even when the try block returned, and even when no catch matched.
After `finally`: a pending `ok` means the method continues to `tail`.
guide.brute_force: Returning as soon as the try block returns skips `finally`, which is exactly the misunderstanding interviewers test.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of catch blocks × hierarchy depth), space O(1) besides the trace.
guide.pitfalls:
- Matching catch types by exact name only.
- Trying later catch blocks after one has run.
- Forgetting that an `Error` is not caught by `catch (Exception e)`.
- Letting a pending return skip `finally`.

java-overload-resolution.title: Which overload is called?
java-overload-resolution.description:
A class has several one-parameter methods named `m`. Given the **declared type** of the argument (a
primitive), decide which one the compiler picks. Java tries three phases and stops at the first that
finds a candidate.

**Phase 1: no boxing.** A parameter type applies if it is the argument type or reachable by **primitive
widening**:

`byte → short → int → long → float → double` and `char → int → long → float → double`.

Pick the applicable type that is **nearest** along that chain.

**Phase 2: boxing.** Box the argument to its wrapper (`byte`→`Byte`, `short`→`Short`, `char`→`Character`,
`int`→`Integer`, `long`→`Long`, `float`→`Float`, `double`→`Double`). A parameter type applies if it is that
wrapper or one of its supertypes. Numeric wrappers: `wrapper → Number → Object`. `Character → Object`.
Pick the nearest.

**Phase 3: varargs.** A parameter written `"T..."` (for a primitive `T`) applies if the argument type is `T`
or widens to `T`. Pick the nearest `T`.

Write `resolve(overloads, arg)`: `overloads` is a list of parameter types (strings such as `"long"`,
`"Integer"`, `"Object"`, `"int..."`), `arg` a primitive type name. Return the chosen parameter type, or
`"compile error"` if nothing applies.

**Examples** `resolve(["long", "Integer"], "int")` → `"long"`; `resolve(["Object", "int..."], "int")` → `"Object"`;
`resolve(["Long"], "int")` → `"compile error"`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Polymorphism, overriding and overloading*: the three phases of overload resolution.
guide.intuition: The compiler prefers the least 'effort': first a plain widening, then boxing, then varargs. Within a phase the closest type wins. So build the list of candidates for each phase in order of closeness and return the first one that exists.
hints: Write the widening chain starting at the argument type. `char` has its own chain and never widens to `short`.
Only if phase 1 finds nothing, try the wrapper, then `Number` (not for `Character`), then `Object`.
Only if phase 2 finds nothing, try `T...` along the widening chain.
guide.brute_force: Checking 'exact match, then wrapper, then anything wider' is the intuitive order and it is wrong: widening `int` to `long` beats boxing to `Integer`.
guide.complexity: Time O(1): the candidate lists have fixed length. Space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Preferring boxing to widening.
- Letting `char` widen to `short`, or `short`/`byte` to `char`.
- Giving `Character` the supertype `Number`.
- Trying varargs before boxing.
guide.follow_up: With two parameters the compiler needs one method that is at least as specific in every position; otherwise the call is ambiguous.

java-dynamic-dispatch.title: Dynamic dispatch, hiding and fields
java-dynamic-dispatch.description:
Given a class hierarchy and `Declared ref = new Runtime();`, decide which class's member is used by
`ref.member`.

`classes` maps a class name to `{"parent": name or None, "methods": [...], "statics": [...], "fields": [...]}`,
listing the instance methods, static methods and fields **declared in that class**.

Write `access(classes, declared, runtime, kind, member)` where `kind` is `"method"`, `"static"` or `"field"`.

1. **Compile-time check.** Search for the member (of that kind) starting at `declared` and going up through
   parents. If it is not found, return `"compile error"`.
2. **Selection.**
   - `"field"` and `"static"`: the class found in step 1 (the declared type decides).
   - `"method"`: search again starting at `runtime` and going up; return the first class that declares it
     (the runtime type decides).

`runtime` is always `declared` or one of its subclasses.

**Example** with `Animal {methods: [speak], statics: [kind], fields: [name]}` and
`Dog extends Animal {methods: [speak, fetch], statics: [kind], fields: [name]}`:
`access(c, "Animal", "Dog", "method", "speak")` → `"Dog"`; `"static", "kind"` → `"Animal"`;
`"field", "name"` → `"Animal"`; `"method", "fetch"` → `"compile error"`.
