java-dynamic-dispatch.starter:
def access(classes, declared, runtime, kind, member):
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Polymorphism, overriding and overloading*: declared type versus runtime type; hiding.
guide.intuition: Two lookups. The compiler looks from the **declared** type to decide whether the access is legal. Only instance methods get a second lookup, from the **runtime** type.
hints: Write one helper that climbs the parent chain from a starting class.
If the helper finds nothing from the declared type, it is a compile error, whatever the object really is.
For methods, call the helper again from the runtime type.
guide.brute_force: Always starting at the runtime type treats fields and static methods as polymorphic. They are not.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** `A {m, n; field x}`, `B extends A {m; static s}`, `C extends B {n; field x}` and
`A ref = new C()`.

- `ref.m()`: legal (found in A). Runtime search from C: C has no `m`, B has → **B**.
- `ref.n()`: legal. Runtime search: C has `n` → **C**.
- `ref.x`: found from the declared type A → **A**, although C declares its own `x`.
- `ref.s()`: `s` is declared in B, which is not visible from A → **compile error**.

```java
class A { String x = "A.x"; String m() { return "A.m"; } static String s() { return "A.s"; } }
class B extends A { String x = "B.x"; @Override String m() { return "B.m"; } static String s() { return "B.s"; } }

A ref = new B();
System.out.println(ref.m());            // B.m   instance method: runtime type
System.out.println(ref.x);              // A.x   field: declared type
System.out.println(ref.s());            // A.s   static: declared type (write A.s() instead)
System.out.println(((B) ref).x);        // B.x   a cast changes the declared type of the expression
```
guide.complexity: Time O(depth of the hierarchy), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Dispatching fields or static methods on the runtime type.
- Allowing a call that only the runtime class declares.
- Returning the declared class for an overridden instance method.

java-init-order.title: Constructor and initialiser order
java-init-order.description:
Work out what a program prints while creating objects.

`classes` maps a class name to
`{"parent": name or None, "static": [labels], "instance": [labels], "ctor": label}`:

- `static`: static initialisers and static field initialisers, in source order;
- `instance`: instance field initialisers and instance initialiser blocks, in source order;
- `ctor`: the constructor body.

`news` is a list of class names: the program executes `new X()` for each, in order. Return the list of
strings printed, each as `"<Class>.<label>"`.

**Rules**

1. A class is **initialised** the first time it is needed: first its superclass (if not yet initialised),
   then its own `static` labels. This happens **once** per class for the whole program.
2. `new X()` initialises `X` (rule 1), then, for each class from the **top** of X's hierarchy **down** to
   `X`: that class's `instance` labels, then its `ctor`.

**Example** `Base {static: [s], instance: [f], ctor: c}`, `Derived extends Base {static: [s], instance: [f], ctor: c}`,
`news = ["Derived", "Derived"]` →
`["Base.s", "Derived.s", "Base.f", "Base.c", "Derived.f", "Derived.c", "Base.f", "Base.c", "Derived.f", "Derived.c"]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Constructors, this and super*: the complete order of initialisation.
guide.intuition: Two phases per `new`. The static phase happens once per class, top of the hierarchy first. The instance phase happens every time, also top first, and within one class the field initialisers come before the constructor body.
hints: Build the chain from the root class down to the class being created.
Keep a set of classes whose static part has already run.
For each class in the chain: all instance labels, then that class's constructor, before moving down.
guide.brute_force: Printing every class's instance initialisers first and all constructors afterwards is a common wrong model: in reality each class finishes (initialisers, then constructor) before its subclass starts.
guide.complexity: Time O(total labels printed), space O(number of classes).
guide.pitfalls:
- Running static initialisers for every `new`.
- Running a subclass's static part before its superclass's.
- Running all field initialisers before any constructor body.
guide.follow_up: This order is why calling an overridable method from a constructor sees the subclass's fields still at their default values.

java-access-check.title: Can this code see that member?
java-access-check.description:
Apply Java's four access levels.

Write `can_access(modifier, same_class, same_package, is_subclass, via_own_type)` returning a boolean.

- `modifier` is `"private"`, `"package"` (no keyword: package-private), `"protected"` or `"public"`.
- `same_class`: the accessing code is inside the class that declares the member.
- `same_package`: the accessing code is in the same package as the declaring class (always true when
  `same_class` is true).
- `is_subclass`: the accessing class is a subclass of the declaring class.
- `via_own_type`: for an instance member reached through a reference `ref.member`, whether the reference's
  type is the accessing class itself or one of its subclasses (as with `this.member`).

**Rules**

| modifier | accessible when |
|---|---|
| `public` | always |
| `protected` | same package, **or** (`is_subclass` **and** `via_own_type`) |
| `package` | same package |
| `private` | same class |

**Example** `can_access("protected", False, False, True, False)` → `False`: a subclass in another package
cannot use a protected member through a reference typed as the superclass.
java-access-check.starter:
def can_access(modifier, same_class, same_package, is_subclass, via_own_type):
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Encapsulation* and *Minimal accessibility and immutable classes*.
guide.intuition: Each level adds one circle of trust: the class, then the package, then subclasses, then everyone. The one subtlety is `protected` outside the package, which works only on references of the subclass's own type.
hints: Handle the four modifiers one at a time.
`protected` includes everything `package` allows.
Outside the package, protected needs both conditions: a subclass, and a reference of its own type.
guide.brute_force: A full 4 × 5 lookup table of situations works, and is how the lesson presents it. Four `if` statements are shorter.
guide.complexity: Time O(1), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Thinking `protected` means 'subclasses only': it also includes the whole package.
- Thinking package-private members are visible to subclasses in other packages.
- Forgetting the own-type restriction on protected access.

java-default-method-conflict.title: Default methods: which implementation wins?
java-default-method-conflict.description:
A class inherits a method `m()` from its superclass chain and from interfaces. Decide which body it gets.

`types` maps a type name to
`{"kind": "class" or "interface", "super": superclass name or None, "interfaces": [names], "m": "body", "abstract" or None}`.

- For a class, `super` is its superclass and `interfaces` the interfaces it implements.
- For an interface, `super` is `None` and `interfaces` are the interfaces it extends.
- `m` says whether the type declares `m` with a body (a concrete method or a default method), declares it
  abstract, or does not declare it.

Write `resolve_default(types, cls)` for a class `cls`. Return the **name of the type** whose body is used,
`"abstract"` if the class ends up with no body, or `"conflict"` if it does not compile until it overrides `m`.

**Rules, in order**

1. **Classes win.** Walk from `cls` up its superclass chain. The first class that declares `m` decides:
   `"body"` → that class's name; `"abstract"` → `"abstract"`.
2. Otherwise collect every interface reachable from `cls` or any of its superclasses (through `interfaces`,
   transitively) that **declares** `m` (body or abstract). Discard any that is a super-interface of another
   collected one (**the most specific wins**).
3. If one interface remains: `"body"` → its name; `"abstract"` → `"abstract"`.
   If several remain: `"conflict"` if at least one has a body, otherwise `"abstract"`. If none: `"abstract"`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Interfaces, default methods, sealed types and pattern matching*: the three resolution rules.
guide.intuition: Java avoids the diamond problem with a strict priority: anything from a class beats anything from an interface; among interfaces a sub-interface beats its super-interfaces; and a real tie is a compile error that the programmer must settle.
hints: Walk the superclass chain first; a declaration in any class there ends the search.
Gather all interfaces, including inherited ones, that mention `m` at all.
Remove any interface that another gathered interface extends; then count what is left.
guide.brute_force: Looking only at the directly implemented interfaces misses defaults inherited through sub-interfaces and cannot tell that a sub-interface overrides its parent.
guide.complexity: Time O(t²) for t types in the worst case (pairwise 'is a super-interface of'); tiny in practice.
guide.pitfalls:
- Letting an interface default beat a method inherited from a superclass.
- Forgetting that an abstract redeclaration in a sub-interface hides the parent's default.
- Reporting a conflict for the diamond where two interfaces merely inherit one default from a common parent.

java-sealed-exhaustive.title: Is the switch over a sealed type exhaustive?
java-sealed-exhaustive.description:
A `sealed` interface lists every permitted subtype, so the compiler can check that a pattern-matching
`switch` covers all possibilities.

`hierarchy` maps a type name to the list of its **permitted direct subtypes**. A type with an empty list is
a **leaf** (a record or final class). Types with a non-empty list are sealed and abstract: no object is
*directly* of such a type, only of some leaf below it.

Write `missing_cases(hierarchy, root, cases)`:

- `root` is the type of the value being switched on;
- `cases` is the list of type patterns in the switch (`case X x ->`). A pattern covers `X` and everything
  below `X`.

Return the **sorted** list of leaf types under `root` that no pattern covers. An empty list means the
switch is exhaustive and needs no `default`.

**Example** `Shape permits Circle, Polygon; Polygon permits Square, Triangle`:
`missing_cases(h, "Shape", ["Circle", "Square"])` → `["Triangle"]`;
`missing_cases(h, "Shape", ["Circle", "Polygon"])` → `[]`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Interfaces, default methods, sealed types and pattern matching*: sealed types and exhaustive switches.
guide.intuition: Only leaves are real values. Each case covers all the leaves at or below its type, so collect the covered leaves and subtract them from the leaves under the root.
hints: Write a helper that collects every leaf at or below a given type.
The covered leaves are the union of that helper over all case types.
Answer: leaves under the root minus the covered ones, sorted. A leaf permitted by two sealed parents is covered if either parent is named.
guide.brute_force: Listing only the root's direct subtypes that lack a case ignores nested sealed types in both directions: a parent pattern covering its children, and children patterns covering a parent.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of types under the root), space O(depth) for the recursion.
guide.pitfalls:
- Looking only one level down.
- Not letting a case on a sealed parent cover all its leaves.
- Reporting sealed (abstract) parents as missing instead of their leaves.

java-gc-reachability.title: Which objects can be garbage collected?
java-gc-reachability.description:
The garbage collector may reclaim an object when no chain of references from a **GC root** reaches it.
Roots are the live local variables on thread stacks and the static fields.

Write `collectable(objects, roots)`:

- `objects` maps each object's id (a string) to the list of ids its fields refer to;
- `roots` is the list of ids referred to directly by roots (it may contain repeats; every id exists).

Return the **sorted** list of ids that are unreachable.

Objects that refer to each other in a cycle are still garbage if no root reaches the cycle: Java does not
count references.

**Example** `collectable({"a": ["b"], "b": [], "c": ["d"], "d": ["c"], "e": ["a"]}, ["a"])` → `["c", "d", "e"]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Object lifecycle, scope and garbage collection*: reachability and mark-and-sweep.
guide.intuition: This is graph reachability. Mark everything you can reach from the roots; whatever stays unmarked is garbage.
hints: Use a stack (or queue) of objects still to visit, starting with the roots.
Skip objects already marked, or a cycle will loop for ever.
The answer is the set of all ids minus the marked ones, sorted.
guide.brute_force: Reference counting ('is anything pointing at me?') is the tempting shortcut. It wrongly keeps cycles alive, and it keeps an object alive merely because another garbage object refers to it.
guide.complexity: Time O(V + E) for V objects and E references, space O(V).
guide.pitfalls:
- Counting references instead of tracing from roots.
- Following only one level of references.
- Recursing without a visited set on cyclic data.

java-equals-hashcode-checker.title: equals / hashCode contract checker
java-equals-hashcode-checker.description:
You are given how a class's `equals` and `hashCode` behave on `n` sample objects, numbered `0..n-1`:

- `eq[i][j]` is the boolean result of `obj_i.equals(obj_j)`;
- `hashes[i]` is `obj_i.hashCode()`.

Write `contract_violations(eq, hashes)` returning the **sorted** list of contract rules that these samples
violate. Possible entries:

| name | violated when |
|---|---|
| `"reflexive"` | some `eq[i][i]` is false |
| `"symmetric"` | some `eq[i][j] != eq[j][i]` |
| `"transitive"` | some `eq[i][j]` and `eq[j][k]` are true but `eq[i][k]` is false |
| `"hash"` | some `eq[i][j]` is true but `hashes[i] != hashes[j]` |

Unequal objects with equal hash codes are **not** a violation (that is an ordinary collision).
Return `[]` when all four rules hold.

**Example** `contract_violations([[True, True], [False, True]], [1, 1])` → `["symmetric"]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Writing equals and hashCode correctly*: the five rules of `equals` and the hash rule.
guide.intuition: Each rule is a statement about all pairs or triples of objects. With a matrix in hand you can test every pair and every triple directly.
hints: Reflexive: look at the diagonal.
Symmetric and hash: loop over all ordered pairs.
Transitive: for every equal pair (i, j), every k equal to j must be equal to i.
guide.brute_force: This *is* the brute force: three nested loops over n samples. For the handful of sample objects a test uses, that is exactly right. Libraries such as EqualsVerifier do the same on generated instances.
guide.complexity: Time O(n³) for the transitivity check, space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Reporting equal hash codes on unequal objects as a violation.
- Checking only `i < j` and missing asymmetry.
- Skipping transitivity.

java-record-equality.title: Record equality
java-record-equality.description:
A record's generated `equals` returns true when the other object is a record of the **same type** and every
pair of corresponding components is equal, where each component is compared by its own rule.

A record value is `[type_name, components]` and each component is `[kind, value]`:

| kind | value | Java comparison |
|---|---|---|
| `"int"` | integer | `==` |
| `"double"` | a **string** such as `"1.5"`, `"0.0"`, `"-0.0"`, `"NaN"` | `Double.compare(a, b) == 0`: `NaN` equals `NaN`, and `0.0` does **not** equal `-0.0` |
| `"String"` | string, or `None` for `null` | `Objects.equals` (two nulls are equal) |
| `"array"` | an integer **identity** | arrays are compared by **reference**: equal only if the identities are the same |
| `"record"` | a nested record value | that record's `equals`, recursively |

Write `records_equal(a, b)` returning a boolean. Two records of the same type always have the same number
and kinds of components.

**Examples**
`records_equal(["Point", [["int", 1], ["int", 2]]], ["Point", [["int", 1], ["int", 2]]])` → `True`;
`records_equal(["Size", [["int", 1]]], ["Point", [["int", 1]]])` → `False`;
`records_equal(["T", [["double", "NaN"]]], ["T", [["double", "NaN"]]])` → `True`.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Classes and objects* (records) and *Writing equals and hashCode correctly*.
guide.intuition: A record is equal to another record of the same class when all components match, and each component kind has its own notion of 'match'. The surprises are `double` (bitwise-style comparison) and arrays (identity, not contents).
hints: Different type names are never equal, even with identical components.
For doubles: handle `NaN` first; then compare numerically **and** compare the signs to tell 0.0 from -0.0.
Recurse for nested records.
guide.brute_force: Python's `==` on the nested lists compares the double strings as text (`"1.50"` vs `"1.5"`) and so gets numerically equal doubles wrong.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** `T(0.0)` vs `T(-0.0)`: neither is NaN; `0.0 == -0.0` numerically, but one text starts with
`-` and the other does not → **False**. Java's `Double.compare(0.0, -0.0)` is not 0, which keeps `equals`
consistent with `hashCode`.

```java
record Point(int x, int y) { }
record Reading(double value) { }
record Blob(int[] data) { }

System.out.println(new Point(1, 2).equals(new Point(1, 2)));                       // true
System.out.println(new Reading(Double.NaN).equals(new Reading(Double.NaN)));      // true
System.out.println(new Reading(0.0).equals(new Reading(-0.0)));                   // false
System.out.println(new Blob(new int[] {1}).equals(new Blob(new int[] {1})));      // false: arrays compare by identity

record SafeBlob(java.util.List<Integer> data) {               // use a List for value equality
    SafeBlob { data = java.util.List.copyOf(data); }          // canonical constructor copies defensively
}
```
guide.complexity: Time O(total number of components, including nested ones), space O(nesting depth).
guide.pitfalls:
- Comparing only the components and ignoring the record type.
- `NaN != NaN` and `0.0 == -0.0`, the primitive `==` rules.
- Expecting two arrays with equal contents to make records equal.

java-immutable-audit.title: Immutable class audit
java-immutable-audit.description:
Check a class description against the five rules for immutable classes.

`cls` is a dictionary:

```
{"final_class": bool, "private_constructors": bool, "setters": [field names with a setter],
 "fields": [{"name": str, "final": bool, "private": bool, "mutable_type": bool,
             "copied_in": bool, "getter": "none" | "direct" | "copy"}, ...]}
```

`mutable_type` says the field refers to a mutable object (an array, a `List`, a `Date`). `copied_in` says
the constructor stores a defensive copy. `getter` says whether a getter exists and whether it returns the
field itself or a copy.

Write `audit(cls)` returning the **sorted** list of violation codes:

| code | when |
|---|---|
| `"SUBCLASSABLE"` | the class is not final **and** its constructors are not all private |
| `"SETTER:<name>"` | for each name in `setters` |
| `"NONFINAL:<name>"` | the field is not final |
| `"NONPRIVATE:<name>"` | the field is not private |
| `"NOCOPYIN:<name>"` | `mutable_type` and not `copied_in` |
| `"LEAK:<name>"` | `mutable_type` and the getter is `"direct"`; **or** `mutable_type` and the field is not private |

`copied_in` and `getter` are ignored for fields of immutable type. An empty list means the class is immutable.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Minimal accessibility and immutable classes*: the five rules.
guide.intuition: Immutability is a checklist. Translate each rule into one condition and collect the codes for every condition that fails.
hints: Start with the class-level rules: subclassing and setters.
Then loop over the fields for `final` and `private`.
The copy rules apply only to fields of mutable types: copy on the way in, and never hand out the original.
guide.brute_force: There is nothing to optimise; the risk is misreading a rule, such as applying the defensive-copy requirement to a `String` field.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of fields), space O(number of violations).
guide.pitfalls:
- Flagging a non-final class whose constructors are all private (it cannot be subclassed from outside).
- Demanding copies for immutable field types.
- Forgetting that a non-private mutable field is itself a leak.

java-string-pool.title: String pool: == versus equals
java-string-pool.description:
Model which `String` variables refer to the **same object**.

`decls` is a list of declarations, in order. Each creates a variable:

| declaration | Java | object |
|---|---|---|
| `[name, "lit", text]` | `String name = "text";` | the pooled string with that text |
| `[name, "new", text]` | `String name = new String("text");` | a brand-new object |
| `[name, "const", t1, t2]` | `String name = "t1" + "t2";` | a compile-time constant: the **pooled** string `t1 + t2` |
| `[name, "concat", var, text]` | `String name = var + "text";` | computed at run time: a **new** object |
| `[name, "intern", var]` | `String name = var.intern();` | the pooled string with `var`'s text |
| `[name, "alias", var]` | `String name = var;` | the same object as `var` |

The pool holds exactly one object per distinct text. `intern` adds the text to the pool if it is not there
yet (as a separate pooled object).

`queries` is a list of `["==", a, b]` or `["equals", a, b]`. Return a list of booleans: `==` is true when
both variables refer to the same object; `equals` when the texts are the same.

**Example** `decls = [["a","lit","java"], ["b","new","java"], ["c","intern","b"], ["p","lit","ja"], ["d","concat","p","va"], ["e","const","ja","va"]]`,
`queries = [["==","a","b"], ["==","a","c"], ["==","a","d"], ["==","a","e"], ["equals","a","d"]]` → `[False, True, False, True, True]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Strings, equals/hashCode, HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap internals*: the string pool.
guide.intuition: Every variable has a text **and** an identity. The pool hands out one identity per text; `new` and run-time concatenation mint fresh identities; an alias copies an identity.
hints: Keep a dictionary from text to the pooled identity.
Literals, constant expressions and `intern()` use the pool.
`==` compares identities; a variable is always `==` to itself and to its aliases, pooled or not.
guide.brute_force: Tracking only 'is this variable pooled?' fails for aliases: two aliases of one `new String` are the same object even though neither is pooled.
guide.complexity: Time O(declarations + queries), space O(distinct texts + objects).
guide.pitfalls:
- Treating run-time concatenation as pooled.
- Forgetting that `intern()` returns the pooled object, not the receiver.
- Returning False for `x == x` when `x` is a heap string.
guide.follow_up: If `p` were declared `final`, `p + "va"` would become a constant expression and `d` would be pooled.

java-hashmap-sim.title: Simulate HashMap: buckets, load factor and resize
java-hashmap-sim.description:
Simulate `java.util.HashMap<Integer, Integer>` with linked-list buckets (no tree bins).

Write `hashmap_sim(capacity, load_factor, ops)`.

- The table starts with `capacity` buckets (a power of two). Keys are Java `int` values; an `Integer`'s
  `hashCode` is the number itself.
- **Spread**: treat the key as an unsigned 32-bit pattern `h` (for a negative key use `key + 2**32`), then
  `hash = h ^ (h >>> 16)` (unsigned shift).
- **Index**: `hash & (n - 1)` where `n` is the current number of buckets.
- `["put", k, v]`: if the bucket already holds key `k`, replace its value. Otherwise append a new entry at the
  **end** of the bucket and increase the size. Then, if `size > n * load_factor`, **resize**.
- **Resize**: double `n`. Each old bucket `i` is split, keeping the entries' relative order: an entry stays at
  index `i` if `hash & old_n` is 0 and otherwise moves to index `i + old_n`.
- `["get", k]`: append the value to the results, or `None` if absent.
- `["remove", k]`: remove the entry if present (size decreases; the table never shrinks). Appends nothing.

Return `[results, table]` where `table` is the final list of buckets, each a list of keys in bucket order.

**Example** `hashmap_sim(4, 0.75, [["put",1,10],["put",5,50],["put",9,90],["put",2,20],["get",5],["get",3]])`
→ `[[50, None], [[], [1, 9], [2], [], [], [5], [], []]]`

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Collections: List, Set, Map and Queue* and *Strings, equals/hashCode, HashMap and ConcurrentHashMap internals*.
guide.intuition: A hash map is an array of small lists. The key's hash picks the list; within the list you compare keys. Growing doubles the array, and because the length is a power of two each entry either stays put or moves up by exactly the old length.
hints: Write `spread(k)` first: mask to 32 bits, then XOR with itself shifted right by 16.
For `put`, search the bucket; replace, or append and bump the size, then test `size > n * load_factor`.
On resize, walk old buckets in order and append each entry to bucket `i` or `i + old_n` depending on `hash & old_n`.
guide.brute_force: Rehashing every entry from scratch with `hash & (new_n - 1)` gives the same buckets. The split form shows why a resize is cheap and order-preserving. An unordered rebuild (collect all, re-insert) also happens to preserve order here because old buckets are visited in index order.
guide.complexity: Average O(1) per operation; a resize costs O(size) but happens only when the size doubles, so the amortised cost stays constant. Space O(size + buckets).
guide.pitfalls:
- Using `%`, which differs for negative keys and skips the spreading step.
- Resizing at `size >= threshold` instead of `>`.
- Resizing on a `put` that only replaced a value.
- Forgetting to mask negative keys to 32 bits before shifting.
guide.follow_up: Real `HashMap` converts a bucket to a red-black tree once it holds 8 entries and the table has at least 64 buckets.

java-multikey-sort.title: Multi-key sort with a Comparator
java-multikey-sort.description:
Sort employee rows the way this Java comparator would:

```java
Comparator.comparing(Employee::dept)
          .thenComparing(Employee::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder())
          .thenComparing(Employee::name)
```

Each row is `[dept, name, salary]` (two strings and an integer). Return a **new** list sorted by:

1. `dept` ascending;
2. then `salary` **descending**;
3. then `name` ascending.

Strings compare as Java's `String.compareTo` does for plain ASCII text: by character code, so every capital
letter sorts before every lower-case letter (Python's string comparison agrees). Do not modify the input.

**Example** `sort_staff([["ops","Bo",30],["dev","Ada",50],["dev","Cy",70],["dev","Al",50]])`
→ `[["dev","Cy",70],["dev","Ada",50],["dev","Al",50],["ops","Bo",30]]`
java-multikey-sort.solution:
def sort_staff(rows):
    return sorted(rows, key=lambda r: (r[0], -r[2], r[1]))

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Sorting with Comparable and Comparator*: `thenComparing` and reversing one key.
guide.intuition: A multi-key comparison looks at the second key only when the first is a tie. In Python that is a tuple key; a descending numeric key is its negation.
hints: Build a key tuple in order of importance.
Negate the salary to reverse only that key.
`sorted` returns a new list and leaves the input alone.
guide.brute_force: Sort three times with a stable sort, least important key first: by name, then by salary descending, then by department. It gives the same result and costs three passes.
guide.complexity: Time O(n log n), space O(n) for the copy.
guide.pitfalls:
- Sorting the salary ascending.
- Putting the keys in the wrong order.
- Reversing the whole sort instead of one key.
- Sorting in place when a new list was asked for.

java-wildcard-assignable.title: Wildcards and PECS
java-wildcard-assignable.description:
Answer three questions about a parameter of type `List<...>` with a wildcard.

`parents` maps each class to its superclass (`None` for `Object`). A type is a subtype of itself and of all
its ancestors.

`param` is `[kind, T]` describing the parameter's type argument:

| `kind` | Java |
|---|---|
| `"exact"` | `List<T>` |
| `"extends"` | `List<? extends T>` |
| `"super"` | `List<? super T>` |
| `"any"` | `List<?>` (T is ignored; it will be `"Object"`) |

Write `wildcard(parents, param, arg, element)` returning `[assignable, can_add, read_type]`:

1. `assignable`: may a `List<arg>` be passed for this parameter?
   exact: `arg == T`; extends: `arg` is a subtype of `T`; super: `T` is a subtype of `arg`; any: always.
2. `can_add`: inside the method, does `list.add(x)` compile for an `x` of static type `element`?
   exact and super: `element` is a subtype of `T`; extends and any: never.
3. `read_type`: the static type of `list.get(0)`: exact and extends: `T`; super and any: `"Object"`.

**Example** with `Integer → Number → Object`:
`wildcard(p, ["extends", "Number"], "Integer", "Integer")` → `[True, False, "Number"]`;
`wildcard(p, ["super", "Integer"], "Number", "Integer")` → `[True, True, "Object"]`.
java-wildcard-assignable.starter:
def wildcard(parents, param, arg, element):
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Generics, wildcards and bounds* and *Bounded wildcards, PECS, varargs and heterogeneous containers*.
guide.intuition: The wildcard says what the compiler knows about the list's element type. `? extends T`: 'some subtype of T', so reading gives a T and adding is forbidden. `? super T`: 'some supertype of T', so adding a T is safe and reading gives only Object.
hints: Write `sub(a, b)`: climb from `a` through `parents` looking for `b`.
Generics are invariant: for `exact`, only the identical type argument is accepted.
For `super`, the subtype test is reversed: `T` must be a subtype of `arg`.
guide.brute_force: There is no cheaper approach; the difficulty is keeping the directions straight. PECS: producer extends, consumer super.
guide.complexity: Time O(depth of the hierarchy), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Treating `List<Integer>` as a `List<Number>`.
- Allowing `add` through `? extends`.
- Reversing the test for `? super`, or returning `T` as its read type.

java-twr-close-order.title: try-with-resources: close order and suppressed exceptions
java-twr-close-order.description:
Simulate one try-with-resources statement.

`resources` is a list, in declaration order, of `[name, open_fails, close_fails]` (two booleans).
`body_throws` says whether the body throws.

**Rules**

1. Open the resources in order. Log `"open <name>"`. If an open fails, log `"open <name> FAILS"` instead:
   that resource and all later ones are **not** opened, the body does **not** run, and the **primary**
   exception is `"open <name>"`.
2. If every resource opened, log `"body"`. If `body_throws`, the primary exception is `"body"`.
3. Close every resource that was successfully opened, in **reverse** order, logging `"close <name>"`.
   If a close fails: when there is no primary exception yet it becomes the primary, `"close <name>"`;
   otherwise it is added to the **suppressed** list, in the order the closes happened.

Return `[log, primary, suppressed]` with `primary` equal to `None` if nothing was thrown.

**Example** `try_with_resources([["A", False, True], ["B", False, True]], True)`
→ `[["open A", "open B", "body", "close B", "close A"], "body", ["close B", "close A"]]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *try-with-resources, multi-catch and custom exceptions*.
guide.intuition: Resources are a stack: opened in order, closed in reverse. The first exception thrown is the one the caller sees; later ones from `close` ride along as suppressed.
hints: Remember which resources were opened successfully.
The body runs only if the opening loop finished without a failure.
Close in reverse; a failing close becomes primary only if nothing has been thrown yet.
guide.brute_force: A hand-written `try`/`finally` with nested blocks does the closing but lets a failure in `close` replace the original exception. Try-with-resources was introduced to fix exactly that.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of resources), space O(number of resources).
guide.pitfalls:
- Closing in declaration order.
- Closing resources that were never opened.
- Letting a close failure replace the body's exception.
- Running the body after a failed open.

java-checked-analyser.title: Checked exceptions: must declare or catch
java-checked-analyser.description:
The compiler rejects a method whose body can throw a **checked** exception that is neither caught nor
declared. Write the check.

`parents` maps each exception type to its superclass; `"Throwable"` maps to `None`. It always contains
`Throwable`, `Exception`, `RuntimeException` and `Error`.

An exception type is **unchecked** if it is `RuntimeException`, `Error`, or a subtype of either. Every other
type (including `Exception` and `Throwable` themselves) is **checked**.

Write `unreported(parents, thrown, caught, declared)`:

- `thrown`: types the body may throw;
- `caught`: types named in `catch` blocks around that code;
- `declared`: types in the method's `throws` clause.

A thrown type is **handled** if it is a subtype of (or equal to) some caught type or some declared type.
Return the **sorted** list (without duplicates) of thrown **checked** types that are not handled. An empty
list means the method compiles.

**Example** with `FileNotFoundException → IOException → Exception`:
`unreported(p, ["FileNotFoundException", "SQLException"], ["IOException"], [])` → `["SQLException"]`
java-checked-analyser.starter:
def unreported(parents, thrown, caught, declared):
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Exceptions: try, catch, finally, checked and unchecked* and *Choosing exceptions*.
guide.intuition: Two filters. First drop everything unchecked. Then, for each remaining type, ask whether some catch or throws entry is the same type **or an ancestor**.
hints: Write `is_a(t, ancestor)` by climbing the `parents` map.
Unchecked means `is_a(t, "RuntimeException")` or `is_a(t, "Error")`.
A handler covers its subtypes, not its supertypes: `catch (FileNotFoundException e)` does not handle an `IOException`.
guide.brute_force: Comparing names for equality ignores the hierarchy both for 'is it unchecked?' and for 'is it handled?'.
guide.complexity: Time O(thrown × (caught + declared) × depth), space O(thrown).
guide.pitfalls:
- Treating `Exception` itself as unchecked.
- Thinking a subclass handler covers its superclass.
- Forgetting that `Error` and its subclasses are unchecked.
- Returning duplicates.

java-stream-pipeline.title: Evaluate a stream pipeline
java-stream-pipeline.description:
Evaluate a Java stream pipeline over a list of integers.

`run_pipeline(data, ops)`: `data` is a list of ints; `ops` is a list of intermediate operations followed by
exactly one terminal operation.

**Intermediate operations**

| op | Java | meaning |
|---|---|---|
| `["filter", "even"]` / `"odd"` / `"positive"` | `.filter(...)` | keep matching elements (positive means `> 0`) |
| `["filter", ["gt", k]]` | `.filter(x -> x > k)` | |
| `["map", ["mul", k]]`, `["map", ["add", k]]`, `["map", "square"]`, `["map", "abs"]` | `.map(...)` | transform each element |
| `["flatMap", "digits"]` | `.flatMap(...)` | replace each element by the decimal digits of its absolute value, most significant first (0 gives `[0]`) |
| `["distinct"]` | `.distinct()` | keep the first occurrence of each value |
| `["sorted"]` | `.sorted()` | ascending |
| `["limit", n]`, `["skip", n]` | `.limit(n)`, `.skip(n)` | |

**Terminal operations**

| op | result |
|---|---|
| `["toList"]` | the list |
| `["count"]` | the number of elements |
| `["sum"]` | `reduce(0, Integer::sum)` |
| `["groupingByCount", "parity"]` | a dict `{"even": n, "odd": m}` containing only the keys that occur |
| `["groupingByCount", ["mod", k]]` | a dict whose keys are `str(x % k)` using Java's remainder (sign of the left operand) |

Ignore overflow. **Example** `run_pipeline([5, 3, 8, 3, 10], [["filter", ["gt", 2]], ["distinct"], ["sorted"], ["limit", 3], ["map", ["mul", 2]], ["toList"]])`
→ `[6, 10, 16]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *The Stream API, collectors and Optional*.
guide.intuition: Although Java runs a pipeline lazily, one element at a time, the **result** is the same as applying each stage to the whole sequence in the order written. So transform a list stage by stage and finish with the terminal operation.
hints: Keep a current list and replace it at every intermediate stage.
`distinct` must keep first occurrences in encounter order: a plain `set` loses the order.
`groupingBy(..., counting())` is a dictionary of counts; for the `mod` key use Java's remainder.
guide.brute_force: Writing a special-case loop for one fixed pipeline works for that pipeline only. A small interpreter over the op list handles every combination.
guide.approach:
**Dry run** `[5, 3, 8, 3, 10]`: `filter > 2` → `[5, 3, 8, 3, 10]`; `distinct` → `[5, 3, 8, 10]`;
`sorted` → `[3, 5, 8, 10]`; `limit 3` → `[3, 5, 8]`; `map ×2` → `[6, 10, 16]`.

Order matters: `limit(3)` **before** `sorted()` would take `[5, 3, 8]` and then sort those three.

```java
List<Integer> result = Stream.of(5, 3, 8, 3, 10)
        .filter(x -> x > 2)
        .distinct()
        .sorted()
        .limit(3)
        .map(x -> x * 2)
        .toList();                                           // [6, 10, 16]

Map<String, Long> byParity = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7)
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(x -> x % 2 == 0 ? "even" : "odd", Collectors.counting()));
// {even=3, odd=4}
```
guide.complexity: Time O(n log n) when `sorted` is present, otherwise O(n) per stage; space O(n).
guide.pitfalls:
- Implementing `distinct` with a set and losing encounter order.
- Reordering stages.
- Using Python's `%` for negative numbers in the `mod` key (Java: `-7 % 3 == -1`).
- Returning a key with count 0 in the grouping result.

java-optional-chain.title: Optional chaining
java-optional-chain.description:
Evaluate `Optional.ofNullable(value).<ops>.orElse(default)`.

`value` is an integer or `None` (Java `null`). `ops` is a list of:

| op | Java | effect on a present value `x` |
|---|---|---|
| `["map", ["add", k]]` | `.map(x -> x + k)` | becomes `x + k` |
| `["map", ["mul", k]]` | `.map(x -> x * k)` | becomes `x * k` |
| `["map", "halfIfEven"]` | `.map(x -> x % 2 == 0 ? x / 2 : null)` | `x / 2` if even; a function returning `null` makes the Optional **empty** |
| `["filter", "positive"]` | `.filter(x -> x > 0)` | empty unless `x > 0` |
| `["filter", ["lt", k]]` | `.filter(x -> x < k)` | empty unless `x < k` |
| `["flatMap", table]` | `.flatMap(x -> lookup(x))` | `table` is a dict with string keys; present with `table[str(x)]` if that key exists, otherwise empty |

Once the Optional is empty, every later operation leaves it empty. Return the final value, or `default` if
the Optional is empty at the end.

**Example** `optional_chain(8, [["map", "halfIfEven"], ["filter", "positive"], ["map", ["add", 1]]], -1)` → `5`;
`optional_chain(7, [["map", "halfIfEven"], ["map", ["add", 1]]], -1)` → `-1`.

guide.prereqs: Lessons *The Stream API, collectors and Optional* and *Varargs, empty collections, Optional returns and documentation*.
guide.intuition: An Optional is a box that is either full or empty. Each operation looks inside only if the box is full; an empty box passes through everything untouched until `orElse` supplies the default.
hints: Track two things: whether a value is present, and the value.
`map` with a function that returns null empties the box.
A present value of 0 is still present: do not test the value's truthiness.
guide.brute_force: Nested `if (x != null)` checks do the same job in Java and grow one level deeper per step. That nesting is what Optional's `map`, `filter` and `flatMap` replace.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of operations), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Using `x or default`, which replaces a legitimate 0.
- Continuing to apply functions after the Optional became empty.
- Forgetting that `map` to null yields empty.

java-builder-validation.title: Builder with validation
java-builder-validation.description:
Simulate a fluent builder: `Pizza.builder().size(30).crust("thin").topping("olive").extraCheese().build()`.

`build_pizza(calls)` receives the method calls in order, each `[method, arg]` or `[method]`:

| call | effect |
|---|---|
| `["size", n]` | set the size in cm (a later call overwrites an earlier one) |
| `["crust", name]` | must be `"classic"`, `"thin"` or `"deep"`; anything else throws **immediately** |
| `["topping", name]` | add a topping (duplicates are kept) |
| `["extraCheese"]` | set the flag |
| `["build"]` | validate and create; calls after `build` are ignored |

Defaults: crust `"classic"`, no toppings, no extra cheese, size unset.

**Return**

- an invalid crust: `"IllegalArgumentException: unknown crust <name>"` (stop at that call);
- at `build`, check in this order and return the first failure:
  1. size never set → `"IllegalStateException: size is required"`
  2. size not in 15..50 → `"IllegalStateException: size must be 15..50 but was <n>"`
  3. more than 5 toppings → `"IllegalStateException: at most 5 toppings but got <k>"`
- on success: `{"size": n, "crust": c, "extraCheese": bool, "toppings": [...]}` (toppings in the order added);
- if `build` is never called: `"not built"`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Static factories, builders, singletons and dependency injection*: the builder pattern.
guide.intuition: The builder is a mutable scratch pad. Setter-like calls only record values; **`build` is the single gate** where rules involving the finished object are checked. A value that is invalid in isolation (an unknown crust) can be rejected at once.
hints: Keep four variables for the builder's state.
Reject a bad crust immediately; record everything else without judging.
At `build`, check in the stated order and return; anything after `build` is ignored.
guide.brute_force: Validating the size inside `size(...)` looks tidy and changes the behaviour: `size(10)` followed by `size(20)` would fail although the pizza finally asked for is valid.
guide.complexity: Time O(number of calls), space O(number of toppings).
guide.pitfalls:
- Validating cross-field rules before `build`.
- Processing calls after `build`.
- Returning the builder's own toppings list instead of a copy.
- Checking the rules in a different order.

tests.expected: IllegalStateException: size must be 15..50 but was 10
IllegalStateException: at most 5 toppings but got 6
IllegalStateException: size must be 15..50 but was 51

java-defensive-copy.title: Defensive copies: does the object leak?
java-defensive-copy.description:
A class `Playlist` holds a list of track numbers. Depending on how carefully it was written, outside code
may be able to change its contents.

`playlist_states(copy_in, copy_out, initial, actions)` simulates:

```java
List<Integer> source = new ArrayList<>(initial);
Playlist p = new Playlist(source);      // stores source itself, or a copy if copy_in
```

then performs `actions`:

| action | Java | effect |
|---|---|---|
| `["mutate_source", v]` | `source.add(v);` | changes the playlist too, **unless** the constructor copied |
| `["mutate_returned", v]` | `p.tracks().add(v);` | `tracks()` returns the internal list, or a fresh copy if `copy_out`; the add goes to whatever was returned |
| `["read"]` | `p.tracks()` | append a **snapshot** of the playlist's internal list to the output |

Return the list of snapshots.

Note the combined case: with `copy_in` false and `copy_out` false, the list returned by `tracks()` **is**
`source`, so `mutate_returned` changes both.

**Example** `playlist_states(False, True, [1], [["mutate_source", 2], ["mutate_returned", 3], ["read"]])` → `[[1, 2]]`
java-defensive-copy.starter:
def playlist_states(copy_in, copy_out, initial, actions):
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Minimal accessibility and immutable classes* and *Parameter checks, defensive copies, signatures and overloading*.
guide.intuition: Model the objects, not the outcomes. There is a `source` list and an `internal` list; they are the same Python object when the constructor did not copy. `tracks()` hands back either `internal` itself or a copy.
hints: Create `internal` as an alias of `source` or as a copy, depending on `copy_in`.
For `mutate_returned`, pick the object that `tracks()` returns and append to that.
A `read` must append a snapshot (`list(internal)`), or later changes will alter earlier output.
guide.brute_force: Tracking only 'does this action reach the playlist?' with flags works until you forget to snapshot: appending the same list object several times makes every earlier snapshot show the final state.
guide.complexity: Time O(actions × list length) because of the snapshots, space O(output).
guide.pitfalls:
- Appending `internal` itself for `read` instead of a snapshot.
- Always copying in the constructor.
- Forgetting that an uncopied `internal` and `source` are one object.

java-enum-state-machine.title: Enum state machine
java-enum-state-machine.description:
An enum with a transition table is the standard way to model a process such as an order's life cycle.

`transitions` maps each state name to the list of states it may move to (every state appears as a key; a
state with an empty list is **terminal**).

Write `run_machine(transitions, start, events)`. `events` is a list of requested target states, processed
in order from the state `start`:

- if the target is **not a state at all**, the result for that event is `"unknown"` and the state is unchanged
  (in Java this would be `Enum.valueOf` throwing `IllegalArgumentException`);
- if the current state may move to the target, the result is `"ok"` and the state changes;
- otherwise the result is `"rejected"` and the state is unchanged.

Return `[final_state, results, is_terminal]`, where `is_terminal` says whether the final state has no
outgoing transitions.

**Example** with `NEW → [PAID, CANCELLED]`, `PAID → [SHIPPED, CANCELLED]`, `SHIPPED → [DELIVERED]`,
`DELIVERED → []`, `CANCELLED → []`:
`run_machine(t, "NEW", ["PAID", "DELIVERED", "SHIPPED", "REFUNDED"])` → `["SHIPPED", ["ok", "rejected", "ok", "unknown"], False]`

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Enums: constants with data and behaviour*: the state machine built from an enum and `EnumSet`.
guide.intuition: Keep one current state. For each request there are three possibilities, tested in a fixed order: the target does not exist; the move is allowed; the move is not allowed.
hints: Check 'is it a state?' before anything else.
Only an allowed move changes the current state.
Terminal means the final state's transition list is empty.
guide.brute_force: A chain of `if (state == NEW && target == PAID) ...` statements grows with every state and is where forgotten cases hide. A table (map from state to allowed targets) scales and can be printed.
guide.complexity: Time O(events × out-degree), or O(events) with sets; space O(events) for the results.
guide.pitfalls:
- Moving to the target even when the transition is rejected.
- Reporting an unknown state as rejected.
- Allowing a self-transition that the table does not list.

java-interleaving-counter.title: Race condition: every possible final count
java-interleaving-counter.description:
`counter++` is not atomic. Each increment is two steps on shared memory:

1. **read** the shared counter into a thread-private temporary;
2. **write** `temporary + 1` back to the shared counter.

`threads` threads each perform `increments` increments, with no synchronisation. The scheduler may switch
threads between **any** two steps. Each thread executes its own steps in order.

Write `possible_totals(threads, increments)` returning the **sorted** list of every final counter value
that some interleaving can produce. The counter starts at 0.

Constraints: `1 <= threads <= 3`, `0 <= increments <= 4`, and the total number of steps is at most 16.

**Examples** `possible_totals(1, 3)` → `[3]`; `possible_totals(2, 1)` → `[1, 2]`;
`possible_totals(2, 2)` → `[2, 3, 4]`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Race conditions, synchronization, deadlock and virtual threads*: the lost update.
guide.intuition: The program's state is the shared counter plus, for each thread, how far it has got and what it holds in its temporary. From any state, any unfinished thread may take the next step. Explore every reachable state and collect the counter values of the finished ones.
hints: Represent a state as `(shared, ((pc, tmp), ...))` so it can go in a set.
An even `pc` is a read (copy shared into tmp); an odd `pc` is a write (shared = tmp + 1).
Use a visited set: many interleavings lead to the same state, and without it the search explodes.
guide.brute_force: Enumerate every ordering of the steps (all ways to interleave the threads' step sequences) and simulate each one. For 2 threads × 4 increments that is 12,870 orderings; for 3 × 2 it is 90,720. The state-space search visits far fewer states because orderings that reach the same state are merged.
guide.complexity: The number of states is at most (max counter + 1) × (steps + 1)^threads × (max tmp + 1)^threads; a few thousand for the allowed sizes. Time and space are proportional to the states visited.
guide.pitfalls:
- Assuming the only outcomes are 'all increments' and 'one thread's worth'.
- Treating the increment as a single step.
- Exploring without memoisation.
- Forgetting the zero-increment case, whose only result is 0.
guide.follow_up: With `synchronized` or `AtomicInteger` the only possible total is `threads × increments`.

java-deadlock-detect.title: Deadlock risk: lock-order inversion
java-deadlock-detect.description:
Two threads can deadlock when one takes lock A then B while another takes B then A. Tools detect this risk
from recorded **traces** by building a **lock-order graph**.

`traces` is a list with one entry per thread; each entry is that thread's sequence of
`["lock", name]` and `["unlock", name]` events, in order. Locks are **reentrant**: locking a lock the thread
already holds adds nothing, and you may assume each such extra lock is matched by an extra unlock (keep a
count per lock).

**Graph.** Whenever a thread acquires a lock `B` that it does not already hold, add an edge `A → B` for every
lock `A` it currently holds. Edges from all threads go into one graph.

**Self-inflicted cycles do not count.** An inversion needs two threads. Record, for every edge, the set of
threads that produced it. There is a deadlock risk if the graph has a cycle `L1 → L2 → ... → Lk → L1`
(k ≥ 2) and the **union** of the thread sets of that cycle's edges contains at least two different threads.

Write `lock_cycle(traces)` returning `True` if such a cycle exists, else `False`.

**Example** thread 0: lock pen, lock paper, unlock paper, unlock pen; thread 1: lock paper, lock pen, unlock
pen, unlock paper → `True`.

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Race conditions, synchronization, deadlock and virtual threads*: the four conditions and lock ordering.
guide.intuition: A deadlock needs a circular wait. Record, for every thread, 'I took B while holding A' as an arrow A → B. If the arrows from different threads form a loop, some schedule can make each thread hold one lock of the loop while waiting for the next.
hints: Replay each trace keeping the list of locks currently held, with a count per lock for reentrancy.
Add an edge from every held lock to a newly acquired one, remembering which thread produced it.
Search for a cycle, carrying the union of the threads seen on the path's edges; the cycle counts when that union has two or more threads.
guide.brute_force: Comparing only pairs of locks (is there both A → B and B → A?) misses cycles of three or more locks, such as the dining philosophers, and wrongly flags a single thread that takes A then B and later B then A.
guide.complexity: Building the graph is O(total events × locks held). The cycle search is exponential in the worst case, which is acceptable for the handful of locks in a trace; real tools use the same graph with smarter searches.
guide.pitfalls:
- Checking only two-lock inversions.
- Flagging a cycle created by one thread alone.
- Adding edges for reentrant acquisitions.
- Using the order locks were first seen instead of what was held at the time.

java-executor-schedule.title: Fixed thread pool in virtual time
java-executor-schedule.description:
Simulate `Executors.newFixedThreadPool(workers)` running tasks that are all submitted at time 0, in order.

- Task `i` (0-based) needs `durations[i]` time units.
- Tasks wait in a FIFO queue. Whenever a worker is free and the queue is not empty, the worker takes the
  task at the head. If several workers are free at the same moment, the one with the **lowest id** takes the
  next task (workers are numbered from 1).

Write `schedule(durations, workers)` returning `[assignments, makespan]`:

- `assignments[i]` is `[worker, start, end]` for task `i`;
- `makespan` is the time at which the last task finishes (0 if there are no tasks).

**Example** `schedule([4, 2, 1, 3, 2], 2)` →
`[[[1, 0, 4], [2, 0, 2], [2, 2, 3], [2, 3, 6], [1, 4, 6]], 6]`
java-executor-schedule.solution:
def schedule(durations, workers):
    import heapq
    free = [(0, w) for w in range(1, workers + 1)]
    heapq.heapify(free)
    out = []
    makespan = 0
    for d in durations:
        t, w = heapq.heappop(free)
        out.append([w, t, t + d])
        makespan = max(makespan, t + d)
        heapq.heappush(free, (t + d, w))
    return [out, makespan]

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Threads, Runnable and ExecutorService*: thread pools, queues and the scheduling model.
guide.intuition: Each task goes to the worker that becomes free earliest. Keep the workers in a priority queue ordered by the time they are next free (and by id to break ties), pop one per task and push it back with its new free time.
hints: Start with every worker free at time 0.
A heap of `(free_time, worker_id)` gives both rules at once.
The task's start is the popped free time; its end is start plus duration.
guide.brute_force: Scan all workers for the smallest free time for every task: O(n × workers). The heap brings it to O(n log workers).
guide.complexity: Time O(n log w) for n tasks and w workers, space O(n + w).
guide.pitfalls:
- Round-robin assignment, which ignores when workers become free.
- Breaking ties toward the highest worker id.
- Returning a makespan of the last task instead of the latest finish.

java-bounded-buffer.title: Producer-consumer with a bounded buffer
java-bounded-buffer.description:
Simulate an `ArrayBlockingQueue` of a given `capacity` shared by producers and consumers.

`script` is a string of `"P"` and `"C"` characters, processed left to right:

- `"P"`: a producer calls `put` with the next item. Items are numbered 1, 2, 3, ... in the order of the `P`
  characters. If the buffer is full, the producer **blocks**: it waits in a FIFO line of blocked producers.
- `"C"`: a consumer calls `take`. If the buffer is empty, the consumer blocks in a FIFO line of blocked
  consumers.

After each character, let blocked operations complete for as long as possible, repeating until nothing
changes: first, while a producer is blocked and the buffer has room, the first blocked producer puts its
item; then, while a consumer is blocked and the buffer is not empty, the first blocked consumer takes the
head item. Repeat both loops until neither makes progress.

Return `[consumed, buffer, blocked_producers, blocked_consumers]`:

- `consumed`: item numbers in the order they were taken;
- `buffer`: the items left in the buffer, head first;
- the two counts of operations still blocked at the end.

**Example** `bounded_buffer(2, "PPPPCC")` → `[[1, 2], [3, 4], 0, 0]`
(after `PPPP` the buffer is `[1, 2]` with two producers blocked; each `C` frees a slot that a blocked producer fills).

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Concurrency utilities, thread-safety levels and lazy initialisation*: `BlockingQueue` and producer-consumer.
guide.intuition: Treat every `put` and `take` as a request that joins a waiting line, then let the lines drain whenever the buffer allows. A blocked operation is not lost; it finishes later, when another operation makes room or supplies an item.
hints: Keep three things: the buffer, the queue of waiting items, and a count of waiting consumers.
After each new request, loop: move waiting items in while there is room; let waiting consumers take while there are items.
Repeat until a full round makes no progress, because a take can unblock a put and the reverse.
guide.brute_force: Dropping an operation that cannot proceed immediately (instead of making it wait) loses items and consumers. That is how a non-blocking `offer`/`poll` behaves, not `put`/`take`.
guide.complexity: Time O(length of the script): each item enters and leaves the buffer at most once. Space O(length).
guide.pitfalls:
- Discarding blocked operations.
- Draining only one waiting operation per step.
- Letting a late consumer overtake one that was already waiting.
- Numbering items by when they enter the buffer instead of by when `put` was called.

java-money-rounding.title: Money: exact arithmetic and HALF_UP rounding

guide.prereqs: Lessons *Primitive types and how numbers are stored* and *Everyday habits: scope, for-each, libraries, money and boxing*.
guide.intuition: Work in whole cents. Integers are exact, so the only place a decision is needed is the single division by 100 for the VAT, and HALF_UP for non-negative numbers is 'add half the divisor, then divide downward'.
hints: Parse `"19.99"` by splitting at the dot: 19 × 100 + 99. Do not go through `float`.
VAT in cents is `subtotal_cents × percent / 100`; compute `(n + 50) // 100` for HALF_UP.
Format with `cents // 100` and `cents % 100` padded to two digits.
guide.brute_force: Using `float` and `round` is shorter and wrong twice over: decimal fractions are not exact in binary, and Python's `round` uses banker's rounding (halves go to the even neighbour).
guide.complexity: Time O(number of lines), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Parsing prices through `float`.
- Truncating the VAT instead of rounding.
- Banker's rounding (`round`) where HALF_UP was specified.
- Formatting 5 cents as `0.5` instead of `0.05`.
guide.follow_up: `RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN` is common in finance because it does not bias totals upward; implement it as a variant.

java-import-resolution.title: Resolve a simple class name
java-import-resolution.starter:
def resolve_name(name, current_pkg, single_imports, wildcard_imports, packages):
    pass

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Packages, imports and the String toolbox*: how the compiler resolves a short name.
guide.intuition: Three levels of priority. A specific import beats the current package, which beats wildcard imports. Only at the last level can two candidates clash, and then the compiler refuses to choose.
hints: Check single-type imports by comparing the text after the last dot.
Then the current package.
Then gather hits from `java.lang` plus the wildcard packages, without duplicates, and count them.
guide.brute_force: Returning the first package that contains the name gets the priority order wrong and never reports ambiguity.
guide.complexity: Time O(imports + size of the packages consulted), space O(1).
guide.pitfalls:
- Preferring a wildcard import to a class in the current package.
- Letting a wildcard reach into sub-packages.
- Forgetting that `java.lang` is always an on-demand import and can take part in an ambiguity.
- Counting the same package twice when it is imported twice.

java-maven-mediation.title: Maven dependency mediation: nearest wins
java-maven-mediation.description:
A Maven project can request two versions of one library through different paths. Maven keeps exactly one,
chosen by **dependency mediation**:

- the version **nearest** to the project in the dependency tree wins;
- at equal depth, the one **declared first** wins;
- the dependencies of a version that **lost** are not followed.

Write `mediate(root_deps, graph)`:

- `root_deps` is the ordered list of the project's direct dependencies, each `"name:version"`;
- `graph` maps `"name:version"` to the ordered list of that artifact's own dependencies (a missing key means
  no dependencies).

Process the tree **breadth-first**: a queue starts with the root dependencies (depth 1) in order. Take the
head: if its `name` is already chosen, skip it entirely; otherwise choose this version and append its
dependencies to the queue in order.

Return the chosen versions as a list of `"name:version"` strings **sorted by name**.

**Example** `mediate(["A:1.0", "B:1.0"], {"A:1.0": ["X:1.0"], "B:1.0": ["C:1.0"], "C:1.0": ["X:2.0"]})`
→ `["A:1.0", "B:1.0", "C:1.0", "X:1.0"]` (X 1.0 is at depth 2, X 2.0 at depth 3).

guide.prereqs: Lesson *Maven, Gradle and the module system*: transitive dependencies and nearest-wins mediation.
guide.intuition: Breadth-first search visits the tree level by level, left to right. The first time a library name comes off the queue is therefore its nearest, earliest-declared occurrence, which is exactly Maven's rule.
hints: Use a queue, not recursion: recursion goes deep before wide and measures the wrong thing.
Decide on the **name**: once a name is chosen, later versions of it are ignored.
Only a chosen version's dependencies join the queue.
guide.brute_force: Depth-first traversal (plain recursion) follows A's entire subtree before looking at B, so a deep transitive dependency of A can beat a direct dependency declared later. Choosing the highest version is Gradle's default, not Maven's.
guide.complexity: Time O(V + E) over the artifacts and dependency edges visited, space O(V).
guide.pitfalls:
- Depth-first traversal.
- Picking the highest version.
- Following the dependencies of a version that lost.
- Keying the decision on `name:version` instead of the name.
